questions.stem: A 73-year-old man presented to the emergency room with slurred speech, vertigo, and incoordination. Exam showed dysarthria, left beating nystagmus, decreased sensation in the left face and right trunk/limbs, and left upper extremity ataxia. Head CT was normal but Brain MRI revealed a medullary infarct. On hospital day 2 he had to be transferred to the ICU for repeated episodes of prolonged central apneas during sleep. Which structures may have been damaged to result in this complication?
questions.stemHtml:
A 73-year-old man presented to the emergency room with slurred speech, vertigo, and incoordination. Exam showed dysarthria, left beating nystagmus, decreased sensation in the left face and right trunk/limbs, and left upper extremity ataxia. Head CT was normal but Brain MRI revealed a medullary infarct. On hospital day 2 he had to be transferred to the ICU for repeated episodes of prolonged central apneas during sleep.
Which structures may have been damaged to result in this complication?

options.label: A
options.text: The dorsal and ventral respiratory groups

questions.answerText: The dorsal and ventral respiratory groups
questions.solution: Correct Option A: The dorsal and ventral respiratory groups The medulla oblongata, specifically the dorsal and ventral respiratory groups, plays a crucial role in the regulation of respiration. The dorsal respiratory group (DRG) is involved in the inspiratory phase of breathing, while the ventral respiratory group (VRG) is responsible for both inspiratory and expiratory activities. These respiratory centers in the medulla receive input from various sensory and motor pathways and coordinate the rhythmic pattern of breathing. When the medulla is affected by an infarct, it can disrupt the functioning of these respiratory centers, leading to abnormal breathing patterns, including central apneas during sleep. Central apneas occur when the brain fails to send the appropriate signals to initiate breathing, resulting in temporary cessation of airflow. Incorrect Options: Option B - The raphe nuclei: The raphe nuclei are located in the brainstem and play a role in various functions, including the regulation of mood, sleep-wake cycle, and pain modulation. Damage to the raphe nuclei may lead to mood disturbances and alterations in the sleep-wake cycle, but it is not directly associated with central apneas during sleep. Option C - The ascending reticular activating system: The ascending reticular activating system (ARAS) is a network of neurons in the brainstem that plays a crucial role in maintaining wakefulness and arousal. It receives sensory input from various sensory pathways and helps to keep the brain alert and responsive to stimuli. Damage to the ARAS can lead to disturbances in consciousness and wakefulness but is not directly linked to central apneas during sleep. Option D - The chemoreceptor trigger zone: The chemoreceptor trigger zone (CTZ) is an area in the brain that detects changes in the blood's chemical composition, such as pH and levels of certain substances like dopamine and serotonin. It is involved in triggering the sensation of nausea and vomiting in response to chemical stimuli. Damage to the CTZ can lead to disturbances in the regulation of nausea and vomiting, but it is not associated with central apneas during sleep. Option E - The pneumotaxic center: The pneumotaxic center, also known as the pontine respiratory group, is located in the pons of the brainstem. It plays a role in regulating the rate and pattern of breathing by modifying the activity of the respiratory centers in the medulla. Damage to the pneumotaxic center can lead to abnormal breathing patterns, but it is not commonly associated with central apneas during sleep. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: Spasticity, a velocity-dependent increase in muscle tone, is a complication of many neurological disorders affecting the brain and/or spinal cord. Baclofen is often used to alleviate spasticity symptoms in neurological disease. Which of the following options best describes its mechanism of action?
questions.stemHtml: Spasticity, a velocity-dependent increase in muscle tone, is a complication of many neurological disorders affecting the brain and/or spinal cord. Baclofen is often used to alleviate spasticity symptoms in neurological disease. Which of the following options best describes its mechanism of action?

options.label: A
options.text: Alpha-2 adrenergic agonist that reduces the release of excitatory neurotransmitters

options.label: D
options.text: Blocks calcium release from the sarcoplasmic reticulum in skeletal muscle cells

questions.solution: Correct Option B: Gamma-aminobutiric acid (GABA)-B receptor agonist Baclofen acts as an agonist at GABA-B receptors in the central nervous system. GABA is an inhibitory neurotransmitter that decreases neuronal excitability. By activating GABA-B receptors, baclofen helps reduce the release of excitatory neurotransmitters, leading to a decrease in the hyperactivity of motor neurons and alleviating spasticity. The GABA-B receptor agonism by baclofen is thought to inhibit the release of neurotransmitters involved in muscle tone regulation, such as glutamate and substance P, resulting in decreased muscle spasticity. Incorrect options: Option A - Alpha-2 adrenergic agonist that reduces the release of excitatory neurotransmitters: This is not the mechanism of baclofen. Alpha-2 adrenergic agonists, like clonidine, reduce sympathetic outflow by acting on alpha-2 adrenergic receptors, but they do not directly affect GABA receptors or spasticity. Option C - Gamma-aminobutiric acid (GABA)-A receptor agonist: Baclofen is not an agonist at GABA-A receptors. GABA-A receptors are also inhibitory receptors, but they have different functions and mechanisms compared to GABA-B receptors. Option D - Blocks calcium release from the sarcoplasmic reticulum in skeletal muscle cells: This mechanism does not apply to baclofen. Blocking calcium release from the sarcoplasmic reticulum would not specifically target spasticity or affect GABA receptors. Option E - Central-acting skeletal muscle relaxant pharmacologically similar to tricyclic antidepressants: Baclofen is a centrally acting skeletal muscle relaxant, but it is not pharmacologically similar to tricyclic antidepressants. Tricyclic antidepressants have a different mechanism of action involving the reuptake inhibition of neurotransmitters like serotonin and norepinephrine, and they are not specifically used for spasticity. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: A 55-year-old woman with a history of rheumatic heart disease and atrial fibrillation wakes from sleep at 6am with right sided weakness and aphasia. She had recently missed a few days of her warfarin. She is assessed in the emergency room at 7am, and her presentation is consistent with acute stroke with an NIHSS of 21. A non-contrast head CT shows no acute intracranial blood. Her INR is 1.8, which makes her ineligible for IV tPA. CT angiography shows a large vessel occlusion in the M1 segment of her left middle cerebral artery. You clarify with her husband that she was asymptomatic when she went to bed at 10pm the night prior. What further investigation is indicated to guide emergent management?
questions.stemHtml:
A 55-year-old woman with a history of rheumatic heart disease and atrial fibrillation wakes from sleep at 6am with right sided weakness and aphasia. She had recently missed a few days of her warfarin. She is assessed in the emergency room at 7am, and her presentation is consistent with acute stroke with an NIHSS of 21. A non-contrast head CT shows no acute intracranial blood. Her INR is 1.8, which makes her ineligible for IV tPA. CT angiography shows a large vessel occlusion in the M1 segment of her left middle cerebral artery. You clarify with her husband that she was asymptomatic when she went to bed at 10pm the night prior.
What further investigation is indicated to guide emergent management?

options.label: D
options.text: MRI brain with and without contrast

questions.solution: Correct Option B: CT perfusion scan In the setting of acute ischemic stroke with a large vessel occlusion, a CT perfusion scan is indicated to assess the extent of the ischemic penumbra and identify salvageable brain tissue. The CT perfusion scan provides valuable information on the cerebral blood flow, cerebral blood volume, and mean transit time, which can help determine the extent of the viable tissue surrounding the core infarct. This information is crucial for guiding emergent management decisions, especially in patients who are ineligible for intravenous tissue plasminogen activator (IV tPA) or thrombectomy. Incorrect Options: Option A - Carotid Duplex ultrasound: Carotid Duplex ultrasound is used to assess the carotid arteries for atherosclerosis and stenosis, which may be relevant in patients with carotid artery disease but is not the most appropriate investigation for this patient's current presentation. Option C - Echocardiography: Echocardiography i s used to evaluate the heart's structure and function and can be helpful in identifying potential sources of cardiac emboli in patients with stroke. However, in this case, the patient's clinical presentation and CT findings point to a large vessel occlusion in the M1 segment of the middle cerebral artery, making a cardiac embolic source less likely. Option D - MRI brain with and without contrast: MRI brain with and without contrast can provide detailed imaging of the brain, but in the acute setting of stroke, a CT perfusion scan is more commonly used for rapid evaluation of cerebral blood flow and tissue viability. Option E - Transcranial Doppler: Transcranial Doppler is a non-invasive imaging technique used to assess blood flow in the intracranial vessels. While it can provide valuable information in certain cases, a CT perfusion scan is the more appropriate investigation in this scenario to evaluate the extent of ischemic penumbra and guide treatment decisions. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: A 17-year-old boy presents with slow and limited eye movements. His past medical history is notable for sensorineural hearing loss as a child status post cochlear implant. A detailed ophthalmological examination shows mild bilateral external ophthalmoplegia with pigmentary retinopathy in both eyes. A lumbar puncture is performed, which shows increased CSF protein with 0 cells and a normal glucose level. Which of the following would be the most important next step in this patient’s evaluation?
questions.stemHtml: A 17-year-old boy presents with slow and limited eye movements. His past medical history is notable for sensorineural hearing loss as a child status post cochlear implant. A detailed ophthalmological examination shows mild bilateral external ophthalmoplegia with pigmentary retinopathy in both eyes. A lumbar puncture is performed, which shows increased CSF protein with 0 cells and a normal glucose level. Which of the following would be the most important next step in this patient’s evaluation?
questions.solution: Correct Option D: Cardiac evaluation The patient's presentation of bilateral external ophthalmoplegia with pigmentary retinopathy is suggestive of a mitochondrial disorder, specifically Kearns-Sayre syndrome (KSS). KSS is a rare mitochondrial myopathy that affects multiple systems, including the eyes, ears, and heart. Given the multisystem involvement in KSS, it is essential to assess cardiac function and structure. Cardiac manifestations in KSS may include conduction abnormalities, cardiomyopathy, and heart block. Regular cardiac evaluation, including electrocardiogram (ECG) and echocardiogram, is crucial in the management of these patients to monitor and detect any cardiac abnormalities. Incorrect Options: Option A - Tensilon testing: Tensilon testing is used in the evaluation of myasthenia gravis, which presents with fluctuating muscle weakness and fatigue. It is not relevant in this case of Kearns-Sayre syndrome. Option B - 3-hour glucose tolerance test: A 3-hour glucose tolerance test is used to assess for diabetes mellitus, which does not appear to be the main concern in this patient's presentation. Option C - TSH and free T4 levels: TSH and free T4 levels are relevant in thyroid function assessment, but there are no indications of thyroid dysfunction in this patient's presentation. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: Which of the following statements regarding single fiber electromyography (SFEMG) in the diagnosis of suspected autoimmune myasthenia gravis (MG) is most accurate?
questions.stemHtml: Which of the following statements regarding single fiber electromyography (SFEMG) in the diagnosis of suspected autoimmune myasthenia gravis (MG) is most accurate?

options.label: A
options.text: It is the most sensitive diagnostic test

options.label: B
options.text: It is the most specific diagnostic test

options.label: C
options.text: It is the most sensitive and the most specific diagnostic test

options.label: D
options.text: It is neither a sensitive nor a specific diagnostic test

questions.answerText: It is the most sensitive diagnostic test
questions.solution: Correct Option A: It is the most sensitive diagnostic test Single fiber electromyography (SFEMG) is a highly sensitive test used to assess the function of the neuromuscular junction in patients suspected of having myasthenia gravis (MG). It is capable of detecting small variations in the timing of muscle fiber action potentials, which are characteristic of neuromuscular transmission disorders like MG. SFEMG is particularly useful for identifying subtle abnormalities in neuromuscular transmission that may not be apparent in other conventional electromyographic tests. Incorrect Options: Option B - It is the most specific diagnostic test: While SFEMG is sensitive for detecting neuromuscular junction abnormalities, it may not be the most specific test for myasthenia gravis. SFEMG can also show abnormalities in other neuromuscular disorders that affect the neuromuscular junction. Therefore, it is not the most specific test for MG, and additional diagnostic evaluations are needed for a definitive diagnosis. Option C - It is the most sensitive and the most specific diagnostic test: This statement is incorrect because while SFEMG is sensitive, it may not be the most specific test for MG. As mentioned earlier, SFEMG can also show abnormalities in other neuromuscular disorders, making it less specific for MG. Option D - It is neither a sensitive nor a specific diagnostic test: This statement is incorrect. SFEMG is indeed a sensitive test for detecting neuromuscular junction abnormalities and is particularly useful for identifying subtle abnormalities in neuromuscular transmission, as seen in MG. However, as mentioned earlier, it may not be the most specific test for MG. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: A medical student in the beginning of 3rd year comes to your office with a complaint of excessive tiredness. She is having trouble concentrating and finds herself dozing off in lectures and during morning rounds. She has always been a “night owl”. In college, she took all afternoon classes so she could sleep in. She would go to bed at 2 AM and get up at 10 or 11 AM and had no trouble falling asleep or staying awake during the day. In the first 2 years of medical school she skipped all morning lectures. However, as a third year she has to be in the hospital no later than 7 AM to pre-round on her patients. She tries to go to bed at 9:00 PM, but lies awake in bed until the middle of the night despite being “exhausted.” She has trouble getting up at 5:30 AM when her alarm goes off. On her days off, she goes to sleep when she’s tired, usually “pretty late,” falls asleep easily and then sleeps in, sometimes until after noon. Her partner says she does not snore or wake up gasping. She has not experienced any episodes of muscle weakness or paralysis. She admits that she is stressed but not more than usual. She drinks socially but denies any illicit drug use. She drinks several cups of coffee throughout the morning but not after 2 PM. What is the most likely diagnosis?

questions.solution: Correct Option D: Delayed Sleep Phase Disorder Delayed Sleep Phase Disorder (DSPD) is a circadian rhythm sleep disorder characterized by a delayed timing of the sleep-wake cycle. Individuals with DSPD have difficulty falling asleep and waking up at the desired or socially acceptable times. Instead, they have a natural tendency to fall asleep and wake up later than what is considered normal. This condition is more common in adolescents and young adults. The medical student's history of being a "night owl," taking afternoon classes in college to sleep in, and having no trouble falling asleep and staying awake during the day when she can follow her preferred sleep schedule, is consistent with the characteristics of DSPD. Additionally, her difficulty falling asleep and staying awake in the morning due to the early hospital schedule further supports this diagnosis. Incorrect Options: Option A - Obstructive sleep apnea: (OSA) is less likely in this case since the medical student denies snoring or waking up gasping. OSA is characterized by repetitive episodes of complete or partial upper airway obstruction during sleep, leading to breathing disturbances and disrupted sleep. Option B - Sleep onset insomnia: Sleep onset insomnia is characterized by difficulty falling asleep at the beginning of the night. This does not fit the medical student's presentation as she has trouble falling asleep at her desired bedtime but does not mention difficulty falling asleep at the beginning of the night. Option C - Behaviorally-induced insufficient sleep syndrome: Behaviorally-induced insufficient sleep syndrome is a condition where inadequate sleep occurs due to voluntary restriction of sleep time. The medical student's presentation is more suggestive of a delayed sleep timing rather than intentional sleep restriction. Option E - Narcolepsy: Narcolepsy is characterized by excessive daytime sleepiness, cataplexy (sudden loss of muscle tone triggered by emotions), sleep paralysis, and vivid dreams during sleep onset. The medical student does not report any of these symptoms, making narcolepsy less likely. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: A 45-year-old woman with a 60 pack-year smoking history presents with signs and symptoms of pancerebellar degeneration. Review of systems include malaise and 20 pounds of unintentional weight loss. There is a family history of breast cancer. You suspect that the patient has paraneoplastic cerebellar degeneration (PCD) after ruling out other etiologies of cerebellar ataxia. She is treated empirically with corticosteroids while awaiting results of her autoantibody testing without any response. Her antibody panel on serum and CSF returns positive for Purkinje cell cytoplasmic antibody type 1 (PCA-1)-IgG (or anti-Yo). A thorough screen including body CT, whole body PET, mammography, breast MRI, and transvaginal ultrasound fails to identify a malignancy. Which of the following statements most accurately reflects accepted recommendations for future cancer screening in this individual?

She is treated empirically with corticosteroids while awaiting results of her autoantibody testing without any response. Her antibody panel on serum and CSF returns positive for Purkinje cell cytoplasmic antibody type 1 (PCA-1)-IgG (or anti-Yo). A thorough screen including body CT, whole body PET, mammography, breast MRI, and transvaginal ultrasound fails to identify a malignancy.
Which of the following statements most accurately reflects accepted recommendations for future cancer screening in this individual?

options.label: A
options.text: Given the strong suspicion for an underlying malignancy the patient should continue to undergo a repeat screen, identical or comparable to her original screen, every 6 months for at least 3-4 years

options.label: B
options.text: Given that her initial screen was negative there is no need for repeat screening for an occult malignancy and this should be treated as a primary autoimmune disorder

options.label: C
options.text: The lack of an occult malignancy makes it more likely that this is not paraneoplastic, and alternative etiologies should be pursued

options.label: D
options.text: Additional screening will add too many delays and the patient should be referred to a surgeon to undergo an exploratory laparotomy given your strong concern for an underlying ovarian cancer

questions.answerText: Given the strong suspicion for an underlying malignancy the patient should continue to undergo a repeat screen, identical or comparable to her original screen, every 6 months for at least 3-4 years

In this case, the presence of anti-Yo antibodies strongly suggests an underlying malignancy. However, in some instances, the tumor may be too small to be detected by standard imaging or may not be evident at the time of initial screening. Therefore, repeat screening is recommended to monitor for the potential development of an occult malignancy that may become detectable over time. Incorrect Options: Option B - Given that her initial screen was negative, there is no need for repeat screening for an occult malignancy, and this should be treated as a primary autoimmune disorder: This option is incorrect because the presence of anti-Yo antibodies indicates a high likelihood of an underlying malignancy, even if the initial screening did not identify the tumor. The risk of an occult malignancy remains, and repeat screening is necessary to detect any potential tumor over time. Option C - The lack of an occult malignancy makes it more likely that this is not paraneoplastic, and alternative etiologies should be pursued: This option is incorrect because the presence of anti-Yo antibodies strongly supports the diagnosis of paraneoplastic cerebellar degeneration, which is often associated with an underlying malignancy. questions.stem: A 48-year-old man reports a 7-year history of progressive asymmetric hearing loss without any additional neurologic deficits by history or examination. When a 256 Hz vibrating tuning fork is placed at the vertex of the head, the patient reports hearing it better in his right ear. When each ear is tested separately, the sound from air conduction is perceived as louder than bone conduction on both sides. Which of the following lesions should be suspected?

When a 256 Hz vibrating tuning fork is placed at the vertex of the head, the patient reports hearing it better in his right ear. When each ear is tested separately, the sound from air conduction is perceived as louder than bone conduction on both sides. Which of the following lesions should be suspected?

options.label: D
options.text: A chronic stroke in the distribution of the anterior inferior cerebellar artery

questions.solution: Correct Options C: Acoustic neuroma on the left The history of progressive asymmetric hearing loss and the findings on Weber and Rinne tests suggest a unilateral sensorineural hearing loss on the left side. The Weber test lateralizes the sound to the left ear, indicating that the patient hears the tuning fork better in the left ear when placed at the vertex. The Rinne test reveals that air conduction is perceived as louder than bone conduction in both ears, ruling out conductive hearing loss. Acoustic neuroma, also known as vestibular schwannoma, is a benign tumor that arises from the Schwann cells of the vestibulocochlear nerve (cranial nerve VIII). It typically presents with progressive unilateral sensorineural hearing loss, tinnitus, and imbalance. The presence of asymmetric hearing loss, lateralization of the Weber test to the left, and normal Rinne test on both sides is highly suggestive of an acoustic neuroma on the left side. Incorrect Options: Option A - Brainstem glioma: This option is less likely as brainstem gliomas would typically present with additional neurologic deficits beyond just asymmetric hearing loss. Option B - Acoustic neuroma on the right: The lateralization of the Weber test to the left ear does not support an acoustic neuroma on the right side. Option D Chronic stroke in the distribution of the anterior inferior cerebellar artery: While a stroke in this artery's distribution could cause hearing loss, it would be less likely to present with a long-standing progressive asymmetric hearing loss without other significant neurological symptoms. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: A 35-year-old heroin addict is brought to the emergency room by a friend with severe muscle rigidity and altered mental status. The friend tells you that when the patient first started to feel ill and before he was encephalopathic, he commented on the fact that he had just been forced to switch to a new dealer. Laboratory evaluation shows lactic acidosis and myoglobinuria. You suspect strychnine poisoning. The neurotoxicity of strychnine is secondary to its effects on which of the following targets?
questions.stemHtml: A 35-year-old heroin addict is brought to the emergency room by a friend with severe muscle rigidity and altered mental status. The friend tells you that when the patient first started to feel ill and before he was encephalopathic, he commented on the fact that he had just been forced to switch to a new dealer. Laboratory evaluation shows lactic acidosis and myoglobinuria. You suspect strychnine poisoning. The neurotoxicity of strychnine is secondary to its effects on which of the following targets?
questions.solution: Correct Option B: Ionotropic glycine receptor Strychnine is a powerful toxin that acts as a competitive antagonist at the glycine receptor, specifically the ionotropic glycine receptor. Glycine receptors are ligand-gated chloride channels that mediate inhibitory neurotransmission in the central nervous system. When glycine binds to its receptor, the channel opens, allowing chloride ions to flow into the cell, resulting in hyperpolarization and inhibition of neuronal activity. In the presence of strychnine, the antagonist, the glycine receptor is blocked, preventing the inhibitory action of glycine. This leads to uncontrolled neuronal excitation and an increase in nerve impulses, causing severe muscle rigidity, convulsions, and spasms. The altered mental status in strychnine poisoning may be a result of the profound impact of muscle rigidity and spasms on the patient's overall neurological function. Incorrect Options: Option A - Metabotropic Glycine Receptor: This receptor type is a different subtype of glycine receptor that acts through intracellular signaling pathways, and strychnine does not target this receptor. Option C - Nicotinic Acetylcholine Receptor: Nicotine primarily affects nicotinic acetylcholine receptors, but it is not the mechanism of action of strychnine poisoning. Option D & E - GABA-A and GABA-B Receptor: Strychnine is not involved in the modulation of gamma-aminobutyric acid (GABA) receptors, which are another type of inhibitory neurotransmitter receptor in the brain. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: A 25-year-old man vacationing in Hawaii presents to the emergency room with lower extremity numbness and weakness. That morning he had his first surfing lesson. He practiced laying prone on the board, paddling, and getting up quickly. After 2 hours, he felt a pop in his back followed by persistent back pain and paresthesias in his legs. This caused him to interrupt the lesson. He paddled back to shore but felt his legs were weak when he was walking to his hotel. Two hour later the weakness and numbness had worsened to the point that he could no longer walk and he trouble urinating. On examination, he had 0-1/5 strength in the bilateral lower extremities and a T-10 sensory level to pinprick but intact vibration and proprioception. A spine MRI showed T2 signal hyperintensity from T8 to the conus, increased signal on diffusion-weighted imaging and corresponding decreased signal on apparent diffusion coefficient mapping. Cerebrospinal fluid showed increased protein and mild elevation in red and white blood cells, with no oligoclonal bands. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis in this case?
questions.stemHtml:
A 25-year-old man vacationing in Hawaii presents to the emergency room with lower extremity numbness and weakness. That morning he had his first surfing lesson. He practiced laying prone on the board, paddling, and getting up quickly. After 2 hours, he felt a pop in his back followed by persistent back pain and paresthesias in his legs. This caused him to interrupt the lesson. He paddled back to shore but felt his legs were weak when he was walking to his hotel. Two hour later the weakness and numbness had worsened to the point that he could no longer walk and he trouble urinating. On examination, he had 0-1/5 strength in the bilateral lower extremities and a T-10 sensory level to pinprick but intact vibration and proprioception. A spine MRI showed T2 signal hyperintensity from T8 to the conus, increased signal on diffusion-weighted imaging and corresponding decreased signal on apparent diffusion coefficient mapping. Cerebrospinal fluid showed increased protein and mild elevation in red and white blood cells, with no oligoclonal bands.
Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis in this case?
questions.solution: Correct Option D: Surfer’s myelopathy Surfer's myelopathy, also known as acute paraplegia of the novice surfer, is a rare but potentially serious condition that occurs after prolonged prone positioning during surfing lessons. It is a non-traumatic, ischemic injury to the spinal cord, usually affecting the thoracic spinal cord. The exact pathophysiology is not fully understood, but it is believed to be related to ischemia of the spinal cord due to sustained flexion and hyperextension of the thoracic spine during surfing. The typical presentation of surfer's myelopathy includes acute onset of back pain and neurological deficits, such as lower extremity weakness, numbness, and sensory changes. The weakness and sensory loss are often bilateral and may progress rapidly, leading to paralysis if not promptly addressed. Symptoms may be severe enough to cause paraplegia and bladder/bowel dysfunction, as seen in this patient. The MRI findings in surfer's myelopathy typically show T2 signal hyperintensity in the affected spinal cord segments, reflecting edema and inflammation. Diffusion-weighted imaging (DWI) may reveal increased signal, while apparent diffusion coefficient (ADC) mapping may show decreased signal, suggesting restricted diffusion in the affected area. Incorrect Options: Option A - West Nile virus infection: West Nile virus infection typically presents with fever, headache, muscle aches, joint pain, and a rash. It can cause neurological complications such as encephalitis or meningitis, but the presentation and MRI findings described in the case are not consistent with West Nile virus. Option B - Multiple sclerosis: Multiple sclerosis is a chronic autoimmune demyelinating disease of the central nervous system. It presents with a wide range of neurological symptoms and typically shows characteristic demyelinating lesions on MRI, such as periventricular plaques and Dawson's fingers. The acute and rapidly progressive nature of the symptoms in this case is not typical of multiple sclerosis. Option C - Idiopathic transverse myelitis: Idiopathic transverse myelitis is an inflammation of the spinal cord that causes motor, sensory, and autonomic dysfunction below the level of the lesion. It is usually a monophasic disorder with sudden onset and rapid progression. The MRI findings in idiopathic transverse myelitis often show a longitudinally extensive lesion involving multiple segments of the spinal cord. The clinical presentation and MRI findings in this case do not match idiopathic transverse myelitis. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: A 38-year-old male with a history of recurrent nephrolithiasis presents to the emergency department with severe pain in his right flank that radiates to his groin and haematuria. He also complains of nausea and vomiting. A non-contrast CT scan confirms the presence of an 15 mm stone in the right kidney. What is the appropriate management for his condition?
questions.stemHtml: A 38-year-old male with a history of recurrent nephrolithiasis presents to the emergency department with severe pain in his right flank that radiates to his groin and haematuria. He also complains of nausea and vomiting. A non-contrast CT scan confirms the presence of an 15 mm stone in the right kidney. What is the appropriate management for his condition?

options.label: A
options.text: Medical management with increased fluid intake and alpha blockers

questions.solution: Correct Option C: Shockwave lithotripsy The most appropriate initial management for a patient with an 15mm kidney stone is shock wave lithotripsy (SWL), a non-invasive technique that uses shock waves to break the stone into smaller fragments that can be passed in the urine. Incorrect Options: Option A - Medical management with increased fluid intake and alpha blockers : Medical management with increased fluid intake and alpha-blockers may be effective for smaller stones, but an 15mm stone is unlikely to pass spontaneously and may require intervention. Option B - Immediate referral for surgical intervention : Immediate referral for surgical intervention may be necessary in certain cases, but it is not the first-line management for most cases of nephrolithiasis. Option D - Ureteroscopy with laser lithotripsy: Ureteroscopy with laser lithotripsy is another treatment option for larger stones, but it is generally reserved for cases where SWL has failed. @Neet_pg_bot

Laboratory findings include serum sodium:142 mmol/L, serum potassium:3.2mmol/L, serum chloride:107 mmol/L, serum Bicarbonate:15 mmol/L. Arterial blood gas shows ph:7.21. Urine analysis findings include pH 5.9, no casts, RBCs, WBCs, or protein. A diagnosis of renal tubular acidosis is suspected. Which of the following is associated with this patient's condition?

Laboratory findings include serum sodium:142 mmol/L, serum potassium:3.2mmol/L, serum chloride:107 mmol/L, serum Bicarbonate:15 mmol/L. Arterial blood gas shows ph:7.21. Urine analysis findings include pH 5.9, no casts, RBCs, WBCs, or protein. A diagnosis of renal tubular acidosis is suspected. Which of the following is associated with this patient's condition?
questions.solution: Correct Option B: Normal anion gap Renal tubular acidosis is due to the inability of the kidney to either excrete hydrogen ions or reabsorbs filtered bicarbonate. There are many types of RTA including type 1 RTA, type 2 RTA, and type 4 RTA. Type 1 RTA is due to the inability of the distal tubule of the nephron to excrete hydrogen ions leading to metabolic acidosis. Causes of RTA include primary causes: familial, and idiopathic. Secondary causes include sickle cell anemia, autoimmune (SLE, Sjogren's), hyperparathyroidism, and Vit. D intoxication, chronic hepatitis, renal transplantation. Anion Gap is used to find the cause of metabolic acidosis. The normal value of the anion gap is 8 to 12 mEq/L. Normal anion gap with metabolic acidosis is due to loss of bicarbonate by the kidney( RTA type 1 and RTA type 2) or gut (Diarrhea). Symptoms include increased respiratory rate, irregular heart rate, muscle weakness, lethargy, constipation, nephrocalcinosis, paralysis, and death. There will be hyperkalaemia due to hyperaldosteronism. Incorrect Options: Option A - High anion gap metabolic acidosis : Conditions with Metabolic acidosis associated with high anion gap include methanol, uraemia, diabetic ketoacidosis, paracetamol, paraldehyde, isoniazid, lactic acidosis, ethylene glycol, salicylates etc. (MUDPILES) . Option C - Decreased anion gap metabolic acidosis : Though not related to acid-base balance, it could signal disease. Conditions with abnormally low anion gap include low serum albumin, increased chloride, hyperkalaemia, hypercalcemia, and multiple myeloma. Option D - Metabolic alkalosis: Metabolic alkalosis results when there is an increase in bicarbonate ions or a decrease in hydrogen ions. In renal tubular acidosis, there i s metabolic acidosis. Some of the causes of metabolic alkalosis are vomiting, diuretics, and hyperaldosteronism . @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: A 67-year-old male undergoes coronary angiography for coronary artery disease. Twenty-four hours after the procedure, the patient complained of decreased urine output. He also has a history of chronic kidney disease. Laboratory analysis reveals an elevated creatinine level. Which of the following is the most likely cause of this patient’s current presentation?
questions.stemHtml: A 67-year-old male undergoes coronary angiography for coronary artery disease. Twenty-four hours after the procedure, the patient complained of decreased urine output. He also has a history of chronic kidney disease. Laboratory analysis reveals an elevated creatinine level. Which of the following is the most likely cause of this patient’s current presentation?
questions.solution: Correct Option A: Contrast nephropathy The above patient who presents with decreased urine output 24 hours after the coronary angiography most likely has contrast-induced nephropathy, which is common in patients with compromised renal function and exposure to contrast medium used in the coronary angiography. Contrast nephropathy Contrast-induced nephropathy is one of the causes of acute kidney injury after intravenous administration of iodinated contrast medium. That is easy usually prevalent in patients with multiple myeloma and those patients with impaired renal function. It is commonly caused by high-dose gadolinium used for MRI or iodinated contrast, or oral sodium phosphate solution. The iodinated contrast medium is usually used for CT angiography or cardiovascular imaging for coronary artery disease. Contrast nephropathy is characterised by an elevation of serum creatinine level 24 to 48 hours after exposure to the contrast medium. The level of serum creatinine peaks within 3 to 5 days and resolves within one week. Following are the mechanisms of contrast-induced nephropathy Hypoxia of the outer medulla of the kidney. Cytotoxic damage to kidney tubules either directly or via the formation of oxygen-free radicals. Transient obstruction of kidney tubule with precipitated contrast medium. Contrast-induced nephropathy can be prevented with adequate hydration along with obtaining renal function tests before performing imaging. The disease can also be prevented using the lowest dose of contrast medium. Incorrect Options: Option B - Acute interstitial nephritis: Acute interstitial nephritis presents with fever, rash, and joint pain along with renal dysfunction. On examination, there are high eosinophil levels in the blood and urine. It usually occurs after the autoimmune or drug-induced injury. This patient has a history of exposure to contrast medium, which contrasts nephropathy as the most likely diagnosis. Option C - Amyloidosis: Amyloidosis doses usually cause chronic renal failure secondary to nephrotic syndrome. The most common cause of secondary amyloidosis is rheumatoid arthritis. This patient presents with acute renal failure rather than chronic renal failure, which in the setting of exposure to contrast makes contrast nephropathy the most likely diagnosis. Option D - IgA Nephropathy: IgA Nephropathy usually presents after the gastrointestinal or upper respiratory tract infection. It is one of the causes of nephrotic syndrome. This patient has no history of upper respiratory or gastrointestinal tract infection, which makes this diagnosis test likely. @Neet_pg_bot

His blood tests reveal a serum potassium level of 6.8 mEq/L. Which medications are commonly used as an ion-binding resin for treating hyperkalemia in CKD patients?
questions.solution: Correct Option C: Sodium polystyrene sulfonate Hyperkalemia is a common chronic kidney disease (CKD) complication and can lead to serious health consequences such as cardiac arrhythmias and cardiac arrest. One treatment option for hyperkalemia is using potassium-binding resins , which exchange sodium ions for potassium ions in the colon and reduce the amount of potassium absorbed into the bloodstream. The most commonly used potassium-binding resin is sodium polystyrene sulfonate (SPS). SPS is administered orally or rectally and can start to work within hours to lower serum potassium levels. However, SPS can cause gastrointestinal side effects such as constipation and can lead to electrolyte imbalances such as hypokalemia or hypomagnesemia. Another potassium-binding resin that can be used to treat hyperkalemia is patiromer. Patiromer is a newer medication administered orally and works by binding to potassium in the colon. It effectively reduces serum potassium levels in patients with hyperkalemia, with fewer gastrointestinal side effects than SPS. Potassium-binding resins such as SPS and patiromer are important treatment options for managing hyperkalemia in CKD patients. However, their use should be carefully monitored to ensure appropriate dosing and to avoid potential side effects. Incorrect Options: Option A - Furosemide : Furosemide is a diuretic that is commonly used in the treatment of hypertension and heart failure. Furosemide can be used to treat hyperkalemia in patients with intact renal function and does not work by binding potassium ions in the gut. Option B - Albuterol : Albuterol is a bronchodilator commonly used to treat asthma and chronic obstructive pulmonary disease. While it can be helpful in the treatment of hyperkalemia by moving potassium ions inside the cells , it is not a potassium-binding resin . Option D - Spironolactone : Spironolactone is a potassium-sparing diuretic that is commonly used in the treatment of hypertension and heart failure. However, it can cause hyperkalemia and is not an appropriate treatment option for patients with hyperkalemia. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.solution: Correct Option D: Post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis The patient presents with the clinical features and investigative findings of post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis. The patient usually presents with coca-cola-coloured urine (haematuria), hypertension and oedema after 10 days of streptococcal throat infection or longer after a streptococcal skin infection. Reduced glomerular filtration rate (GFR), proteinuria and oliguria can also occur. Light microscopic findings include diffuse proliferation of endothelial and mesangial cells and infiltration by neutrophils and macrophages . Subendothelial deposits are seen on immunofluorescence. It usually resolves spontaneously within 10-14 days . Management is with fluid and sodium restriction, diuretics, and hypotensive agents. Incorrect Options: Option A - Membranous nephropathy: Membranous nephropathy is the most common cause of nephrotic syndrome in adults . Symptoms and signs of membranous nephropathy include proteinuria, oedema, and hypercholesterolemia. It occurs due to granular subepithelial IgG deposits. There is diffuse thickening of the glomerular basement membrane on renal biopsy. Haematuria and hypertension are absent and there is no link with throat infection. Option B - Minimal change of disease: Minimal change disease, also known as lipoid nephrosis . It is characterised by severe proteinuria in children. Proteinuria results in oedema and intravascular volume depletion . No change is seen with light microscopy, but the fusion of podocyte foot processes is seen with electron microscopy. Haematuria and hypertension are absent and there is no link with throat infection. Option C - IgA nephropathy: IgA nephropathy is an autoimmune kidney disease . The clinical features of IgA nephropathy are similar to post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis. However, it usually occurs within 1 week of an upper respiratory tract infection . questions.solution: Correct Option A: Renal artery stenosis Renal artery stenosis is a common cause of acute kidney injury, especially in patients with underlying cardiovascular risk factors such as hypertension and diabetes. Option D - Renal artery embolism: Renal artery embolism is another rare cause of acute kidney injury , which occurs when a blood clot dislodges from a distant site and lodges in the renal artery. questions.stem: A 45-year-old man with a history of renal transplant 10 years ago has presented to the hospital with elevated creatinine levels and decreased urine output. In addition, the patient has a history of non-compliance with immunosuppressive medications, as noted in his previous follow-up appointments. A biopsy confirms the diagnosis of acute rejection. What is the best initial management of acute rejection?
questions.stemHtml: A 45-year-old man with a history of renal transplant 10 years ago has presented to the hospital with elevated creatinine levels and decreased urine output. In addition, the patient has a history of non-compliance with immunosuppressive medications, as noted in his previous follow-up appointments. A biopsy confirms the diagnosis of acute rejection. What is the best initial management of acute rejection?

options.label: A
options.text: Increase the dose of the current immunosuppressive medications

questions.solution: Correct Option B: Administer high-dose corticosteroids Acute kidney rejection is a type of immune-mediated injury that can occur in the early post-transplant period, usually within the first 6 months, but it can also occur at any time after transplantation. The clinical presentation of AKR can be variable and depends on the severity of rejection. Some common symptoms and signs include: Decreased urine output or oliguria Elevated serum creatinine levels Fever Flu-like symptoms such as malaise, nausea, and vomiting Abdominal pain Hematuria Hypertension The gold standard for diagnosis is a kidney biopsy which shows infiltration of inflammatory cells, particularly T cells, in the interstitial spaces between the renal tubules. High-dose corticosteroids are the first-line treatment for acute rejection. The corticosteroids work by suppressing the immune system and decreasing inflammation. They are typically administered intravenously and can effectively reverse the rejection process. Incorrect Options: Option A - Increase the dose of the current immunosuppressive medications: While increasing the dose of current immunosuppressive medications may be beneficial in some cases, it is not the first-line treatment for acute rejection. This approach is more appropriate for preventing rejection or treating chronic rejection. Option C - Initiate treatment with anti-thymocyte globulin (ATG ): ATG is a polyclonal antibody that targets and destroys T cells. It can treat acute rejection in patients who do not respond to corticosteroids or have severe rejection. However, ATG is associated with a higher risk of infection and other adverse effects. Option D - Restart the patient on hemodialysis: Hemodialysis is not a treatment for acute rejection. It may be necessary if the rejection is severe and the kidney no longer functions, but it is not a first-line treatment option. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.solution: Correct Option A: Allergic interstitial nephritis The patient's symptoms include flank pain, myalgia, reddish discolouration of urine, laboratory findings of hematuria (blood in urine), proteinuria (protein in urine), and an elevated serum creatinine level consistent with Allergic interstitial nephritis (AIN ). It is acu te tubulointerstitial nephritis, usually due to a hypersensitivity reaction to drugs, including antibiotics such as penicillin . The time frame for symptom onset can vary, with symptoms appearing anywhere from 1 week to 9 months after exposure to the drug, but most commonly 2-3 months later. The severity of symptoms does not typically depend on the dosage of the drug . Eosinophiluria, an increase in eosinophils in the urine, can often be seen on urine microscopy in patients with AIN. If AIN is suspected, the first step in management should be to discontinue the offending medication, including penicillin , if the patient is still taking it. Intravenous fluids should be administered to help maintain proper fluid and electrolyte balance. In more severe cases, corticosteroids may be used to reduce inflammation and aid in the recovery of kidney function. Option C - Acute tubular necrosis (ATN): ATN is acute kidney injury typically caused by ischemia or nephrotoxic drugs . It can present with oliguria, electrolyte imbalances, muddy brown cast, epithelial cell casts, myoglobinuria, hemoglobinuria and increased serum creatinine . It presents with gross hematuria, proteinuria, oedema, and hypertension . While the patient does have hematuria and proteinuria, the timing and lack of other symptoms make PSGN less likely. questions.stem: A 58 year male with AML, who completed induction therapy with standard dose cytarabine and idarubicin is admitted with c/o fever (38.6 degrees C). CBC demonstrates a leukocyte count of 1100/μL and an absolute neutrophil count of 90/μL. He reports a stiff neck, headache and develops nausea. What is the minimum platelet count you would require in this patient to proceed with a diagnostic lumbar puncture?
questions.stemHtml: A 58 year male with AML, who completed induction therapy with standard dose cytarabine and idarubicin is admitted with c/o fever (38.6 degrees C). CBC demonstrates a leukocyte count of 1100/μL and an absolute neutrophil count of 90/μL. He reports a stiff neck, headache and develops nausea. What is the minimum platelet count you would require in this patient to proceed with a diagnostic lumbar puncture?
questions.solution: Correct Option C : ≤ 50,000/μL The AABB (formerly the American Association of Blood Banks) developed guidelines for the appropriate use of platelet transfusion (Kauffman et al., Ann Intern Med 2015). These published recommendations were based on randomized clinical trials and observational studies (published between 1900 and September 2014) reporting clinical outcomes on patients receiving prophylactic or therapeutic platelet transfusions. The guidelines make the following 6 recommendations: Hospitalized patients with therapy-induced hypoproliferative thrombocytopenia should be transfused prophylactically to reduce the risk for spontaneous bleeding for a platelet count of ≤ 10,000/μL. In these patients, The AABB recommends transfusing up to a single apheresis unit or equivalent. Patients undergoing elective central venous catheter placement should receive prophylactic platelet transfusion for a platelet count ≤ 20,000/μL. Patients having elective diagnostic lumbar puncture should receive prophylactic platelet transfusion for a platelet count less ≤ 50,000/μL. Patients undergoing major elective non-neuraxial surgery should receive prophylactic platelet transfusion for a platelet count less ≤ 50,000/μL. Patients who are non-thrombocytopenic and undergo cardiac surgery with cardiopulmonary bypass should NOT receive routine prophylactic platelet transfusion. However, those patients undergoing bypass surgery who experience perioperative bleeding with thrombocytopenia and/or evidence of platelet dysfunction should receive prophylactic platelet transfusion. The AABB cannot recommend for or against platelet transfusion for patients receiving antiplatelet therapy who have intracranial hemorrhage (traumatic or spontaneous). @Neet_pg_bot

Correct Option C : ≤ 50,000/μL

The AABB (formerly the American Association of Blood Banks) developed guidelines for the appropriate use of platelet transfusion (Kauffman et al., Ann Intern Med 2015). These published recommendations were based on randomized clinical trials and observational studies (published between 1900 and September 2014) reporting clinical outcomes on patients receiving prophylactic or therapeutic platelet transfusions.

The guidelines make the following 6 recommendations:

  1. Hospitalized patients with therapy-induced hypoproliferative thrombocytopenia should be transfused prophylactically to reduce the risk for spontaneous bleeding for a platelet count of ≤ 10,000/μL. In these patients, The AABB recommends transfusing up to a single apheresis unit or equivalent.
  2. Patients undergoing elective central venous catheter placement should receive prophylactic platelet transfusion for a platelet count ≤ 20,000/μL.
  3. Patients having elective diagnostic lumbar puncture should receive prophylactic platelet transfusion for a platelet count less ≤ 50,000/μL.
  4. Patients undergoing major elective non-neuraxial surgery should receive prophylactic platelet transfusion for a platelet count less ≤ 50,000/μL.
  5. Patients who are non-thrombocytopenic and undergo cardiac surgery with cardiopulmonary bypass should NOT receive routine prophylactic platelet transfusion. However, those patients undergoing bypass surgery who experience perioperative bleeding with thrombocytopenia and/or evidence of platelet dysfunction should receive prophylactic platelet transfusion.
  6. The AABB cannot recommend for or against platelet transfusion for patients receiving antiplatelet therapy who have intracranial hemorrhage (traumatic or spontaneous).

questions.solution: Correct Option D: Treat with either plasmapheresis or immunoglobulins Plasmapheresis and intravenous immunoglobulin therapy (IVIG) are equally effective. It is important to treat acute inflammatory polyneuropathy (Guillain-Barre Syndrome) before it potentially results in hypoventilation and hypoxic/anoxic brain injury. Incorrect Options: Option A - Monitor closely without treatment since spontaneous resolution of symptoms will eventually begin: Although the natural course of acute inflammatory polyneuropathy includes spontaneous resolution, severe consequences can result if a patient has significant respiratory compromise. Blood gas does not indicate an impending respiratory decline and is suggestive of hypoventilation, This includes a relatively low pH (normal 7.38-7.42), low normal oxygenation (75-100 mmHg), mildly elevated arterial CO2 (38-42 mmHg) and early signs of metabolic compensation with an elevated bicarbonate level (22-28mEq/L). The expected CO2 in this patient would be 62 mmHg with expected HCO3 of 21. Option B - Treat with high-dose steroids: Steroid treatment is no longer justified for acute inflammatory polyneuropathy since randomized controlled studies have failed to show benefit. In chronic inflammatory polyneuropathy, steroids are of considerable therapeutic value. Option C - Intubate prophylactically: Although the patient is showing early clinical signs of respiratory difficulty, his or her arterial blood gas does not support intubation, and the initiation of plasmapheresis or IVIG may prevent further decline. In addition, the condition may begin to resolve at any time during the course of the disease. The generally accepted parameters used which suggest impending respiratory arrest, and the need to intubate are: A forced vital capacity <20 mL/kg, a maximum inspiratory pressure <30 cmH2O, or a maximum expiratory pressure <40 cmH2O. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stemHtml:
A 55-year-old female is diagnosed with carcinoid syndrome after presentation with diarrhoea. She is treated with octreotide 50 micrograms TDS and is noted to have a marked improvement in her diarrhoea. She is converted to long-acting octreotide 30 mg monthly but begins to notice that the stools have become rather bulky, pale and oily.
Which of the following is the most likely explanation for this?
questions.solution: a" data-dictid="938890efd616927771870f4a611546">exocrine insufficiency, a side effect of the octreotide therapy and caused by inhibition of pancreatic enzyme secretion. Diverticular disease: Diverticular disease refers to the presence of small pouches (diverticula) that can form in the walls of the colon. While diverticular disease can cause changes in bowel habits, such as diarrhea or constipation, it is not typically associated with bulky, pale, and oily stools. Extensive terminal ileal disease: Extensive disease affecting the terminal ileum (the last part of the small intestine) can lead to malabsorption of nutrients, but it does not specifically cause oily stools. Instead, it may result in diarrhea and malabsorption-related symptoms. Gallstones: Gallstones can obstruct the bile ducts and cause a condition known as "cholestasis," where bile flow from the liver to the intestine is impaired. Cholestasis can lead to pale stools, but it does not typically cause oily or bulky stools. Pancreatic exocrine deficiency: The symptoms of bulky, pale, and oily stools (steatorrhea) are characteristic of malabsorption due to pancreatic exocrine deficiency. The pancreas produces digestive enzymes, including lipase, which help break down fats in the intestine. questions.stem: A 21-year-old male presents to the medical outpatient department with complaints of a painless ulcer on his penis for one week. He is sexually active, has multiple sex partners and doesn't use a condom. Examination reveals a firm, shallow ulcer having a smooth base and bilateral nontender inguinal adenopathy. Which of the following is the diagnostic investigation for the patient’s current pathology?
questions.stemHtml: A 21-year-old male presents to the medical outpatient department with complaints of a painless ulcer on his penis for one week. He is sexually active, has multiple sex partners and doesn't use a condom. Examination reveals a firm, shallow ulcer having a smooth base and bilateral nontender inguinal adenopathy. Which of the following is the diagnostic investigation for the patient’s current pathology?
questions.solution: Correct Option B: Dark field microscopy This is a case of primary syphilis in which the patient presents with complaints of a painless ulcer on his penis for one week. The patient further gives the history that he is sexually active has multiple sex partner s and he doesn't use a condom. The examination of the patient is done which reveals a firm, shallow ulcer having a smooth base and bilateral nontender inguinal adenopathy . All these signs and symptoms along with the examinational findings suggest primary syphilis. Syphilis is a sexually transmitted infection which is caused due to treponema pallidum. It usually progresses to four successive stages if left untreated. Dark field microscopy is the diagnostic investigation for primary syphilis. Darkfield microscopy is one of the confirmatory tests for syphilis in which a sample is taken from the skin lesion and is directly visualized under darkfield microscopy. It helps in direct visualization of serious exudate of treponema pallidum. Incorrect Options: Option A: Obtain a bacterial culture Obtaining bacterial culture is usually the diagnostic investigation in most bacterial infections. Although syphilis is caused by treponema pallidum , this bacterium is an obligate intracellular organism which can't be cultured in the laboratory . Option C: Tzanck test Tzanck test is a test which is usually done for the diagnosis of skin lesions which are caused due to herpes virus infection, cytomegalovirus, or varicella zoster infection. It has no role in the diagnosis of syphilis. Option D: Urine polymerase chain reaction A urine polymerase chain reaction is usually done to detect an organism by amplifying its RNA or DNA. However, a urine PCR is done to diagnose many diseases such as chlamydia trachomatis or gonorrhoea infection but in syphilis, the PCR requires a sample from the lesion. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: A colleague states that her patient may have a restrictive ventilatory defect. Which value from the patient’s pulmonary function tests would be required to confirm this finding?
questions.stemHtml: A colleague states that her patient may have a restrictive ventilatory defect. Which value from the patient’s pulmonary function tests would be required to confirm this finding?
questions.solution: Correct Option C: Total lung capacity The definition of a restrictive ventilatory defect is a reduced total lung capacity. Incorrect Options: Option A - FEV1: FEV1 can be reduced because of either an obstructive or a restrictive ventilatory defect. Option B - Functional residual capacity: Most restrictive ventilatory defects result in decreased functional residual capacity; however, in neuromuscular weakness (one of the causes of restrictive ventilatory defects), functional residual capacity is actually increased because of decreased expiratory muscle tone. Therefore, a decreased functional residual capacity does not define restriction. Option D - FEV1/FVC ratio: While a decreased FVC with a normal or even high FEV1/FVC ratio can suggest a restrictive ventilatory defect, this pattern does not define a restrictive ventilatory defect. An obstructive ventilatory defect is defined as a reduced FEV1/FVC ratio. Patients can have combined obstructive and restrictive ventilatory defects with both a reduced FEV1/FVC ratio and a reduced total lung capacity. Pathologic processes that affect both the lung parenchyma (causing restriction) and the airways (causing obstruction) like sarcoidosis can demonstrate this combined pattern. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: A 35-year-old man visits his primary care doctor complaining of tiredness, appetite loss, and stomach pain that has been going on for the previous two weeks. He denies having had a fever, jaundice, or recent travel. He has an unremarkable medical history and doesn't use any drugs. He appears icteric and pale upon closer inspection. On palpation, the liver is swollen and painful. Laboratory tests show increased liver enzymes, bilirubin, and high HBsAg and HBe antigen results (HBeAg). Which diagnosis is more likely?
questions.stemHtml: A 35-year-old man visits his primary care doctor complaining of tiredness, appetite loss, and stomach pain that has been going on for the previous two weeks. He denies having had a fever, jaundice, or recent travel. He has an unremarkable medical history and doesn't use any drugs. He appears icteric and pale upon closer inspection. On palpation, the liver is swollen and painful. Laboratory tests show increased liver enzymes, bilirubin, and high HBsAg and HBe antigen results (HBeAg). Which diagnosis is more likely?
questions.solution: Correct Option B: Acute hepatitis B infection The clinical picture of this patient and the results of the laboratory tests are consistent with acute hepatitis B infection. A viral infection called hepatitis B predominantly damages the liver and can result in either acute or chronic liver disease. Blood and other bodily fluids, particularly perinatal transmission, and sexual contact, are the main ways the virus spreads. The symptoms of acute hepatitis B infection, which include fatigue, appetite loss, abdominal pain, and jaundice, are characterized by HBsAg and increased liver enzymes. HBeAg in the blood also signals vigorous viral replication and a high risk of transmission to others. Incorrect Options: Option A: Acute hepatitis A infection Acute hepatitis A infection is typically self-limited and does not lead to chronic liver disease. It is transmitted by the faecal-oral method. It is characterized by severe jaundice, very high liver function tests, severe nausea, vomiting and diarrhoea. Option C: Chronic hepatitis B infection Chronic hepatitis B infection can result from hepatitis B. Hepatitis B virus (HBV)-induced chronic hepatitis B infection is a long-term viral infection that can result in liver inflammation. When contaminated blood or bodily fluids are present, such as during unprotected intercourse or needle sharing, the virus can be spread. While some sufferers of chronic hepatitis B might not exhibit any symptoms, others might struggle with exhaustion, nausea, loss of appetite, and abdominal pain. Serious liver issues, including liver cancer and cirrhosis (liver scarring), can result from chronic hepatitis B. Option D: Nonalcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD) NAFLD symptoms include fatigue, pain or discomfort in the upper right abdomen and enlarged liver. This patient’s presentation is not consistent with NAFLD. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: Infants who weigh <2000 grams have a suboptimal immunological response to the hepatitis B vaccine. In cases in which the mother expresses positivity for hepatitis B surface antigen, which of the following is the recommended management?
questions.stemHtml: Infants who weigh &lt;2000 grams have a suboptimal immunological response to the hepatitis B vaccine. In cases in which the mother expresses positivity for hepatitis B surface antigen, which of the following is the recommended management?

options.label: A
options.text: Administer hepatitis B vaccination by 12 hours, which will count as 1 of the 3 doses in the series

options.label: B
options.text: Administer hepatitis B vaccination within 12 hours and HBIG within 7 days, with the vaccination not counting toward the 3-part series

options.label: C
options.text: Administer hepatitis B vaccination 1 month after birth, once the immunological response to the vaccine matures

options.label: D
options.text: Administer hepatitis B vaccination to the infant at any point before hospital discharge

questions.answerText: Administer hepatitis B vaccination within 12 hours and HBIG within 7 days, with the vaccination not counting toward the 3-part series
questions.solution: Correct Option: B. Administer hepatitis B vaccination within 12 hours and HBIG within 7 days, with the vaccination not counting toward the 3-part series For infants <2000 grams in weight, studies have shown a suboptimal immunological response to the administration of hepatitis B vaccination at birth. However, in special circumstances in which the mother’s hepatitis B status is not known or is positive, the hepatitis B vaccination should be administered to the infant within 12 hours regardless of weight, and HBIG should be administered within 7 days if the mother expresses positivity for hepatitis B surface antigen during laboratory testing. The vaccination is not counted toward the doses in the 3 part series, and the first official dose should be given at 1 month of age, the second at 2-3 months, and the third at 6 months. Incorrect Options: Option A- Administer hepatitis B vaccination by 12 hours, which will count as 1 of the 3 doses in the series: Although the hepatitis B vaccination should be administered within 12 hours in infants <2000 grams born to hepatitis B-positive mothers, this vaccination does not count in the 3-part series due to the suboptimal immune response in these infants. Option C-Administer hepatitis B vaccination 1 month after birth, once the immunological response to the vaccine matures: Within 12 hours, a single dose should be given. This is not counted toward the 3-part vaccination series. Option D- Administer hepatitis B vaccination to the infant at any point before hospital discharge: If the mother was negative for hepatitis B and the infant weighed ≥2000 grams, then the first vaccination in the series would be given at any point before hospital discharge. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: A 58-year-old male with refractory B-cell acute lymphoid leukemia (B-ALL, dx 6 months ago) is admitted to ICU with acute neutropenic septic shock secondary to klebsiella bacteremia. He is currently on ECOG 1910 regimen and takes Lovenox for atrial fibrillation. He has a history of pulmonary embolism. There no other associated symptoms like chest pain, cough, nausea, vomiting, rash, or headaches. However, he reports 1-2 days of diarrhea. The patient is intubated due to inability to compensate for severe metabolic acidosis due to suspected likely gut translocation. Echocardiogram shows mildly dilated LA. LVEF is 60%. He has no valvular abnormalities and normal ventricular contractility. Chest X-ray shows increasing airspace opacities, bilateral lung bases, and midzone alveolar edema. Pneumonia is excluded. The patient has a persistent, small left pleural effusion with associated slight basal atelectasis. Arterial blood gas shows an oxygen tension of 198 mmHg with a fraction of inspired oxygen of 0.8. What information is lacking that precludes a diagnosis of acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS)?

Echocardiogram shows mildly dilated LA. LVEF is 60%. He has no valvular abnormalities and normal ventricular contractility. Chest X-ray shows increasing airspace opacities, bilateral lung bases, and midzone alveolar edema. Pneumonia is excluded. The patient has a persistent, small left pleural effusion with associated slight basal atelectasis. Arterial blood gas shows an oxygen tension of 198 mmHg with a fraction of inspired oxygen of 0.8. What information is lacking that precludes a diagnosis of acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS)?

options.label: A
options.text: There is no indication of CPAP or PEEP

options.label: B
options.text: Berlin definition includes only new respiratory failure and not worsening respiratory symptoms

options.label: C
options.text: Any pleural effusion would prevent attaching any importance to lung opacitie

options.label: D
options.text: Cardiac failure cannot be excluded without information of pulmonary arterial wedge pressure.

questions.answerText: There is no indication of CPAP or PEEP
questions.solution: Correct Option A: There is no indication of CPAP or PEEP. This information does not provide any information of PEEP. The following are the components of the Berlin criteria for ERDS diagnosis that have superseded the American-European Consensus Conference (AECC definition): Presence of acute hypoxemic respiratory failure criteria Onset within 1 week of insult, or new (within 7 days) or worsening respiratory symptoms Bilateral airspace disease on chest X-ray or computed tomography not fully explained by effusions, lobar or lung collapse, or nodules Cardiac failure not the primary cause of acute hypoxemic respiratory failure This definition has many limitations. For instance, the term "acute onset" is not defined (i.e. within hours, days, or weeks); the degree of hypoxemia may vary significantly depending on PEEP levels; the agreement in interpretation of radiological findings remains modest, even between experts. Threshold values of PCWP <18 mmHg (in the case of measurement) are not always discriminative, since many patients with ARDS exhibit values >18 mmHg, due to increased intrathoracic pressure or fluid overload after resuscitation. Finally, the term ALI is commonly misused, referring to both patients with 200 < FiO2 < 300 mmHg and those suffering from ARDS with FiO2 < 200. Incorrect Options: Option B - Berlin definition includes only new respiratory failure and not worsening respiratory symptoms: Berlin criteria also includes worsening criteria Option C - Any pleural effusion would prevent attaching any importance to lung opacities: Bilateral airspace disease on chest X-ray or computed tomography not fully explained by effusions, lobar or lung collapse, or nodules. Option D - Cardiac failure cannot be excluded without information of pulmonary arterial wedge pressure: Cardiac failure can be ruled out by pulmonary capillary wedge pressure. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.answerText: Asbestos exposure increases the risk of lung cancer associated with cigarette smoke exposure
questions.solution: Correct Option A : Asbestos exposure increases the risk of lung cancer associated with cigarette smoke exposure. The risk of lung cancer associated with exposure to both asbestos and cigarette smoke appears to be multiplicative. A 1979 report in the Annals of the New York Academy of Science showed that asbestos is associated with a 6-fold increase, cigarette smoking with an 11-fold increase, and both cigarette smoke and asbestos exposure with a 59-fold increase in the risk of lung cancer. Incorrect Options: Option B - Coughing, sputum production, and wheezing are the most common presenting symptoms: Dyspnea is the most common presenting symptom of asbestos-induced lung disease. Coughing, sputum production, and wheezing are unusual presenting symptoms and, if present, tend to be due to cigarette smoke rather than asbestos exposure. Although some investigators have questioned the causal relationship between asbestosis and bronchogenic carcinoma, most studies have demonstrated a clear association between these entities. Option C - Antinuclear antibody, rheumatoid factor, and erythrocyte sedimentation rate have prognostic implications: Antinuclear antibody and rheumatoid factor may be present, as may a raised erythrocyte sedimentation rate, but these are not clinically useful because they are nonspecific and not related to disease severity. Option D - Cigarette exposure does not increase the risk of lung cancer associated with asbestos exposure: Cigarette smoking is associated with an 11-fold increase in the risk of lung cancer. @Neet_pg_bot

Serologic testing confirms a diagnosis of tularemia. Treatment with Doxycycline is initiated. Which of the following is the correct mechanism of action for this treatment?

options.label: A
options.text: Inactivation of enzymes in the bacterial cell membrane

options.label: B
options.text: Reversible binding to the bacterial 30S ribosomal subunit

options.label: C
options.text: Inhibition of enzymes involved in tetrahydrofolic acid synthesis

questions.answerText: Reversible binding to the bacterial 30S ribosomal subunit
questions.solution: Correct Option B: Reversible binding to the bacterial 30S ribosomal subunit. Doxycycline is a tetracycline antibiotic. The mechanism of action is through reversible binding to the bacterial 30S ribosomal subunit, leading eventually to inhibition of bacterial protein synthesis. The tetracyclines are broad-spectrum bacteriostatic antibiotics used to treat many aerobic gram-positive and gram-negative infections. They are also active against atypical bacteria such as Rickettsia species. The most common side effects involve the gastrointestinal system. In general, tetracyclines should not be used in pregnant women (unless other medications are not effective or contraindicated) due to possible fetal toxicity, or in young children under 8 years of age due to the potential for tooth discoloration. Incorrect Options: Option A- Inactivation of enzymes in the bacterial cell membrane: Beta-lactam antibiotics such as penicillin inhibit bacterial growth by inactivating enzymes located in the bacterial cell wall. Option C-Inhibition of enzymes involved in tetrahydrofolic acid synthesis: Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole works by inhibiting enzymes involved in the synthesis of tetrahydrofolic acid, which subsequently inhibits DNA synthesis. Option D-Binding to the 50S ribosomal subunit and inhibiting protein synthesis: Macrolides (e.g. azithromycin, erythromycin) inhibit bacterial protein synthesis by binding the bacterial 50S subunit. @Neet_pg_bot

Incorrect Options:

Option A- Inactivation of enzymes in the bacterial cell membrane: Beta-lactam antibiotics such as penicillin inhibit bacterial growth by inactivating enzymes located in the bacterial cell wall.

Option C-Inhibition of enzymes involved in tetrahydrofolic acid synthesis: Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole works by inhibiting enzymes involved in the synthesis of tetrahydrofolic acid, which subsequently inhibits DNA synthesis.

questions.stemHtml: A 58-year-old male reports to his physician with shortness of breath, wheezing, and worsening dyspnea on exertion. He also admits smoking (over 3 packs of cigarettes per day for the past 42 years). He was never intubated but has been admitted several times for acute management of COPD with bronchodilators. Physical examination reveals poor air movement in the lungs. Chest radiograph shows flattening of the diaphragm and an increased anterior-posterior chest diameter. He undergoes pulmonary function testing. Which of the following patterns will be seen on his pulmonary function tests?

options.label: C
options.text: Normal forced expiratory volume in 1 sec/forced vital capacity (FEV1/FVC)

questions.solution: Correct Option D: Reduced FEV1/FVC The forced expiratory volume in 1 second/forced vital capacity (FEV1/FVC) is a ratio that is effort dependent and responds positively to increased expiratory effort. FEV1 is the volume of air forcefully expired with each breath during the first second. FVC is the maximal volume of air expelled with deep expiration. Residual volume (RV) is the volume of air remaining in the lungs after a maximal expiratory effort. Vital capacity (VC) is the maximal volume of air that may be expelled from the lungs following a maximal inspiration. A reduced FEV1/FVC is suggestive of obstructive airway disease. The reduced ratio implies decreased airway emptying because of air trapping. This patient probably has chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) from smoking. Incorrect Options: Option A - Decreased residual volume/total lung capacity (RV/TLC): COPD would cause an increase in RV/TLC, not a decrease as a result of air trapping since the terminal airways close before all the air is expelled. Option B - Decreased RV: RV will be increased because of air trapping. Option C - Normal forced expiratory volume in 1 sec/forced vital capacity (FEV1/FVC): The obstructive pattern should cause a decrease in FEV1/FVC. The flow loop would show characteristic scooping because of this phenomenon. @Neet_pg_bot

Correct Option D: Reduced FEV1/FVC

  • The forced expiratory volume in 1 second/forced vital capacity (FEV1/FVC) is a ratio that is effort dependent and responds positively to increased expiratory effort. FEV1 is the volume of air forcefully expired with each breath during the first second. FVC is the maximal volume of air expelled with deep expiration. Residual volume (RV) is the volume of air remaining in the lungs after a maximal expiratory effort. Vital capacity (VC) is the maximal volume of air that may be expelled from the lungs following a maximal inspiration. A reduced FEV1/FVC is suggestive of obstructive airway disease. The reduced ratio implies decreased airway emptying because of air trapping. This patient probably has chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) from smoking.

Incorrect Options:

Option A - Decreased residual volume/total lung capacity (RV/TLC): COPD would cause an increase in RV/TLC, not a decrease as a result of air trapping since the terminal airways close before all the air is expelled.

Option B - Decreased RV: RV will be increased because of air trapping.

Option C - Normal forced expiratory volume in 1 sec/forced vital capacity (FEV1/FVC): The obstructive pattern should cause a decrease in FEV1/FVC. The flow loop would show characteristic scooping because of this phenomenon.

questions.stem: A 52-year-old man walks into the ER with rapid heavy breathing and complains of dyspnea and persistent fatigue. On physical examination, he has an increased anteroposterior diameter of the chest and hypertrophy of the accessory respiratory muscles. No cyanosis is evident. He relates a history of regularly smoking 2.5 packs of cigarettes per day for 29 years. He also reports episodes of nonproductive coughing, each lasting a few days, but denies asthma attacks. Blood gas analysis shows minimal hypoxemia and normal CO2. Respiratory exam suggests reduced forced expiratory volume/second (FEV1), markedly increased residual volume (RV), and increased total lung capacity (TLC). Which of the following explains the most prominent pathogenesis of this patient's symptoms?
