Blood gas analysis shows minimal hypoxemia and normal CO2. Respiratory exam suggests reduced forced expiratory volume/second (FEV1), markedly increased residual volume (RV), and increased total lung capacity (TLC). Which of the following explains the most prominent pathogenesis of this patient's symptoms?
questions.solution: Correct Option B: Loss of elastic recoil This patient is a classic "pink puffer” with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD). COPD refers to overlapping clinical conditions from a varying combination of emphysema, asthma, bronchiectasis, and chronic bronchitis. If emphysema is predominant, patients with COPD have severe dyspnea (“puffers”), scanty sputum production, and nearly normal arterial partial pressure of oxygen with no cyanosis (“pink”). Loss of elastic recoil is the most prominent characteristic of emphysema, which is due to the destruction of alveolar walls and enlargement of airspaces distal to terminal bronchioles. Destruction of the pulmonary elastic fibers leads to increased resistance to airflow, which is reflected by a decreased FEV1. The lungs become hyperinflated, and while total pulmonary capacity increases, the functioning lung parenchyma decreases. The barrel-chest deformity of this patient is a consequence, not a cause, of the underlying pathology (overexpansion of lungs). Incorrect Options: Option A - Airway obstruction: Airway obstruction is the most prevalent characteristic of patients who have COPD with chronic bronchitis ("blue bloaters"). Decreased PaO2 leads to cyanosis, and bronchitis causes abundant sputum production. Pulmonary hypertension and right ventricular overload produce peripheral edema (bloaters). Option C - Chest wall deformity: Deformities of the chest like severe kyphoscoliosis and obesity can lead to interstitial fibrosis, ultimately prompting restrictive pulmonary disease. Restrictive pulmonary disease leads to decreased total lung compliance and a reduction in all respiratory volumes. Option D - Interstitial infiltration: Interstitial infiltration can lead to interstitial fibrosis, ultimately prompting restrictive pulmonary disease. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: Which of the following is characteristic of HIV retinopathy?
questions.stemHtml: Which of the following is characteristic of HIV retinopathy?

options.label: A
options.text: Yellow-white lesions that are first seen in the peripheral aspects of the orbit and spread along vascular arcades

options.label: B
options.text: Cotton wool spots, hemorrhages, and microaneurysms

options.label: D
options.text: Optic neuritis and macular exudates that may occur in a star pattern

questions.answerText: Cotton wool spots, hemorrhages, and microaneurysms
questions.solution: Correct Option B: Cotton wool spots, hemorrhages, and microaneurysms HIV retinopathy commonly presents with cotton wool spots, hemorrhages, and microaneurysms. HIV endothelial infection is thought to cause cotton-wool spots and these vascular alterations, as well as accelerate the aging process leading to earlier onset of macular degeneration and cataracts. In the early stages, CMV retinitis may have a similar appearance on fundoscopy. Early CMV retinitis can start as a small, white retinal infiltrate that might look very similar to a cotton-wool spot. In cases in which the appearance is harder to differentiate, serial fundoscopic examinations would be appropriate, because CMV retinitis will progress without treatment. In HIV-infected patients, the following organisms are known to infect the eye: cytomegalovirus (CMV), herpes zoster virus, Toxoplasma gondii, Mycobacterium tuberculosis, Mycobacterium avium intracellulare, Cryptococcus neoformans, Pneumocystis jirovecii, Histoplasma capsulatum, Candida species, molluscum contagiosum virus, and microsporidia. Organisms that infect the posterior segment and cause significant visual morbidity are CMV, herpes zoster virus, and T. gondii. Incorrect Options: Option A- Yellow-white lesions that are first seen in the peripheral aspects of the orbit and spread along vascular arcades: CMV retinopathy commonly presents with papillary involvement, retinal hemorrhages, and yellow-white lesions that are first seen in the peripheral aspects of the orbit and subsequently spread along the vascular arcades. Option C-Progressive outer retinal necrosis: Necrotizing herpes retinitis (HZO) may develop in immunocompromised patients such as those who have HIV. An ophthalmologic examination is significant for progressive outer retinal necrosis (PORN). PORN differs from CMV retinitis in that it progresses rapidly and with very little vitreous inflammation on exam. Option D- Optic neuritis and macular exudates that may occur in a star pattern: Atypical toxoplasmosis is observed in immunodeficient individuals and frequently presents with optic neuritis and macular exudates that may occur in a star pattern. A macular scar results from inflammation of the optic nerve and is most commonly idiopathic, but certain infectious diseases (including toxoplasmosis, syphilis, Lyme disease, and cat scratch disease) should be considered. Toxoplasmosis is the most common causative agent of retinochoroidal inflammatory lesions, so their observation should raise suspicion. @Neet_pg_bot

His fingernails and toenails have a yellowish discoloration, are brittle, and are significant for hyperkeratosis. In addition, the patient has 3+ lymphedema in each leg. Chest X-ray was significant for bilateral pleural effusions. Which of the following most likely plays a role in this patient’s presentation?
questions.stemHtml: A 47-year-old male presents with dyspnea and swelling of the legs. The patient has a history of recurrent lung infections. Chest X-ray was significant for bilateral pleural effusions. Which of the following most likely plays a role in this patient’s presentation?
questions.solution: Correct Option A: Lymphatic drainage abnormalities Yellow nail syndrome (YNS) presents with a triad of yellow nails, lymphedema, and pulmonary abnormalities- often pleural effusions, bronchiectasis, and infections. YNS has a complex pathophysiology, with lymphatic drainage abnormalities playing a significant role. The commonality of lymphedema, which is a presenting clinical sign in two-thirds of YNS patients, in addition to the common occurrence of chylothorax does support a more likely pathology in the lymphatic drainage system. The lymphatic abnormality is likely functional, and related to the recurrent lung infections in this patient population inducing a constant state of systemic inflammation. Incorrect Options: Option B . Microangiopathy: Microangiopathy is occasionally present at the nail beds of patients with YNS. Option C . Hypoproteinemia: There is no current studies which support the hypothesis that YNS is the result of hypoproteinemia. Option D. Ciliary dyskinesia: Ciliary dyskinesia as a pathological mechanism of the recurrent sinopulmonary infections was once considered, but has since been disproven. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.solution: Correct Option D: Praziquantel Praziquantel is the therapy of choice for the eradication of schistosomiasis infections and lacks significant side effects, allowing it to be used during pregnancy and in children. Incorrect Options: Option A- Oxamniquine: Is a therapeutic option in cases of schistosomiasis with resistance to praziquantel, but use during pregnancy is contraindicated. Option B- Benznidazole: Is not a component of the current guidelines regarding the treatment of schistosomiasis; it is the mainstay of therapy in the treatment of chagas disease. Option C-Praziquantel plus mefloquine: Studies have shown combination therapy using mefloquine and praziquantel fails to produce an increase in effectiveness toward schistosomiasis, so this therapeutic option would not make sense. @Neet_pg_bot

Lungs are clear to auscultation. A skin examination reveals pink nodular lesions on the extensor surface of both arms. questions.solution: Correct Option A : This syndrome is most likely associated with a good prognosis and spontaneous remission. This patient has signs that are highly suggestive of sarcoidosis. The history of a rash on the lower extremities and the presence of nodular erythematous lesions on the arms are compatible with erythema nodosum. Patients with sarcoidosis may present with a syndrome characterized by hilar adenopathy, a fever, arthralgias, and erythema nodosum (Lofgren's syndrome). This syndrome is typically associated with a good prognosis and spontaneous resolution. Incorrect Options: Option B - The presence of a normal angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) level practically excludes this diagnosis: Although many patients with untreated sarcoidosis have elevated levels of serum ACE, the absence of an elevated level does not rule out the presence of the disease. Option D - A chest CT most likely will show evidence of fibrosis and traction bronchiectasis: This patient's chest radiograph shows mild reticular changes compatible with stage II sarcoidosis. questions.solution: Correct Option A: Alström syndrome Alström syndrome (AS) is a rare autosomal recessive disease characterised by multiorgan dysfunction. The key features are childhood obesity, blindness due to congenital retinal dystrophy, and sensorineural hearing loss. Associated endocrinologic features include hyperinsulinaemia, early-onset type 2 diabetes, and hypertriglyceridemia. Thus, AS shares several features with the common metabolic syndrome, namely obesity, hyperinsulinaemia, and hypertriglyceridaemia. Mutations in the ALMS1 gene have been found to be causative for AS with a total of 79 disease-causing mutations having been described. Further symptoms described in relation to AS include progressive sensorineural hearing loss, a dilated cardiomyopathy in over 60% of cases, developmental delays in 50 % of cases leading to learning difficulties in up to 30% of cases. questions.solution: Correct Option C: Methylphenidate HCL This addresses the drug-drug interaction of agents commonly used in narcolepsy. Modafinil and armodafinil cause enzyme induction of CYP3A4, thereby increasing the metabolism of ethinylestradiol. This reduces the efficacy of the patient's OCP. For this reason, methylphenidate is the most appropriate option for this patient, unless the estrogen component of the OCP is increased (in which case modafinil or armodafinil can be used). Incorrect Options: Option A - Modafinil: Modafinil will reduce OCP efficacy. Option B - Armodafinil: Armodafinil will reduce OCP efficacy. Option D - Venlafaxine: Venlafaxine is a serotonin and norepinephrine reuptake inhibitor that is only used for the treatment of cataplexy in patients with narcolepsy. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: A patient comes to the Emergency Department by ambulance after a syncopal episode that occurred while he was combining several insecticides found in his mother’s garage. He reports vomiting, diarrhoea, and chest tightness. On exam, his heart rate is 60 beats/minute and blood pressure is 100/80 mm Hg. He is diaphoretic with pinpoint pupils. His eyes are watery and he appears to be drooling slightly. Muscle fasciculations are noted in the biceps and quadriceps muscles. Which of the following is the most likely etiology of his symptoms?
questions.stemHtml:
A patient comes to the Emergency Department by ambulance after a syncopal episode that occurred while he was combining several insecticides found in his mother’s garage. He reports vomiting, diarrhoea, and chest tightness.
On exam, his heart rate is 60 beats/minute and blood pressure is 100/80 mm Hg. He is diaphoretic with pinpoint pupils. His eyes are watery and he appears to be drooling slightly. Muscle fasciculations are noted in the biceps and quadriceps muscles.
Which of the following is the most likely etiology of his symptoms?

options.label: A
options.text: Binding of acetylcholine agonists to post-junctional receptors.

options.label: C
options.text: Analogue of acetylcholine that works at the post-synaptic junction.

questions.solution: Correct Option D: Irreversible inhibition of acetylcholinesterase This patient exhibits features of the toxidrome associated with organophosphate poisoning, which probably occurred due to exposure to fertilizer or insecticide. Organophosphates can be inhaled, absorbed through the skin, or ingested and absorbed through the gastrointestinal (GI) tract. Acetylcholinesterase converts acetylcholine to the inactive metabolites acetate and choline. Organophosphates bind to acetylcholinesterase in red blood cells, inactivating the enzyme. Irreversible inhibition of acetylcholinesterase results in the stimulation of the post-synaptic acetylcholine receptors, leading to excess acetylcholine at the neural synapse and neuromuscular junction. The organophosphate toxidrome can be recalled by using the mnemonic “SLUDGE,” which represents salivation, lacrimation, urination, defecation, and emesis, caused by accumulation of acetylcholine at muscarinic nerve synapses in the parasympathetic and sympathetic nervous system. Overstimulation of nicotinic receptors at the neuromuscular junction results in fasciculations and myoclonic jerks. Another useful mnemonic Organophosphate poisoning: "DUMBBELSS”: Tx: Atropine, Pralidoxime Diarrhea Urination Miosis Bradycardia Bronchospasm Excitation of skeletal muscle and CNS Lacrimation Salivation Sweating Acetylcholine agonists include medications like pilocarpine, used to treat open-angle glaucoma. Treatment of severe organophosphate toxicity includes the administration of supplemental oxygen, intubation, and administration of atropine and pralidoxime Incorrect Options: Option A - Binding of acetylcholine agonists to post-junctional receptors: Atropine and scopolamine bind acetylcholine receptors at the presynaptic acetylcholine receptors to block the activity of acetylcholine. Option B - Reversible inhibition of acetylcholinesterase: Reversible acetylcholinesterase inhibitors are associated with improvement of function in patients with Alzheimer’s disease and myasthenia gravis, but these drugs can also cause nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, confusion, dizziness, and arrhythmias. They are not used for the treatment of organophosphate toxicity. Option C - Analogue of acetylcholine that works at the post-synaptic junction: Succinylcholine is an analog of acetylcholine that works at the post-synaptic junction. It should be avoided when performing rapid sequence intubation in patients with organophosphate toxicity. @Neet_pg_bot

  • Acetylcholinesterase converts acetylcholine to the inactive metabolites acetate and choline. Organophosphates bind to acetylcholinesterase in red blood cells, inactivating the enzyme. Irreversible inhibition of acetylcholinesterase results in the stimulation of the post-synaptic acetylcholine receptors, leading to excess acetylcholine at the neural synapse and neuromuscular junction.
  • The organophosphate toxidrome can be recalled by using the mnemonic “SLUDGE,” which represents salivation, lacrimation, urination, defecation, and emesis, caused by accumulation of acetylcholine at muscarinic nerve synapses in the parasympathetic and sympathetic nervous system. Overstimulation of nicotinic receptors at the neuromuscular junction results in fasciculations and myoclonic jerks.

Another useful mnemonic

Organophosphate poisoning: "DUMBBELSS”: Tx: Atropine, Pralidoxime

  • Diarrhea
  • Urination
  • Miosis
  • Bradycardia
  • Bronchospasm
  • Excitation of skeletal muscle and CNS
  • Lacrimation
  • Salivation
  • Sweating

Option C - Analogue of acetylcholine that works at the post-synaptic junction: Succinylcholine is an analog of acetylcholine that works at the post-synaptic junction. It should be avoided when performing rapid sequence intubation in patients with organophosphate toxicity.

questions.stem: A 37-year-old man is admitted for septic shock secondary to cellulitis. He is started on IV fluids and broad-spectrum antibiotics after blood cultures are sent. He appears confused and agitated. Vitals are as follows: BP 90/40, HR 120 bpm, and RR 20. Which variable should be monitored as a good indicator of prognosis?
questions.stemHtml: A 37-year-old man is admitted for septic shock secondary to cellulitis. He is started on IV fluids and broad-spectrum antibiotics after blood cultures are sent. He appears confused and agitated. Vitals are as follows: BP 90/40, HR 120 bpm, and RR 20. Which variable should be monitored as a good indicator of prognosis?
questions.solution: Correct Option C: lactic acid Lactate levels can be monitored to assess hypoperfusion and prognosis. Shock is characterized by inadequate tissue perfusion, leading to increased anaerobic metabolism and lactic acidosis. This increase in lactate may be buffered at first, so ABG may not reflect this change in PH in early shock. Lactate can be used as a marker for tissue hypoperfusion, and a serum level >4 mmol/L strongly correlates with sepsis. Lactate clearance correlates with improved tissue perfusion. As lactate levels increase from 2 to 8 mmol/L, mortality rates also increase from 10-90%. Higher lactate clearance is associated with better prognosis and outcomes. Incorrect Options: Option A- Arterial blood gas: Is used to assess acid-base homeostasis, but it may not accurately reflect the rise in lactate levels and the decrease in PH in early shock. Thus, it is not a good indicator of prognosis. Option B- Brain natriuretic peptide: Is useful in cardiogenic shock, as it indicates CHF and can help determine prognosis. Option D- CBC: Is useful to confirm an underlying infection if the WBC is elevated, as the platelet count may be low in the setting of coagulopathy and sepsis. It can also help exclude anemia. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: A 71-year-old male undergoes a home sleep test for evaluation of snoring, witnessed apneas, and daytime sleepiness. The patient has a history of mild dementia. His BMI is 30, and he has a Mallampati score of 3 and an enlarged tongue. Despite sleeping over 8.5 hours per night, the patient reports a bothersome level of daytime sleepiness and has an Epworth sleepiness scale score of 16. His home sleep test reveals an AHI of 3.2. The oximetry signal on the device stopped working 30 minutes into the study. What is the next step in the management of this patient?
questions.stemHtml: A 71-year-old male undergoes a home sleep test for evaluation of snoring, witnessed apneas, and daytime sleepiness. The patient has a history of mild dementia. His BMI is 30, and he has a Mallampati score of 3 and an enlarged tongue. Despite sleeping over 8.5 hours per night, the patient reports a bothersome level of daytime sleepiness and has an Epworth sleepiness scale score of 16. His home sleep test reveals an AHI of 3.2. The oximetry signal on the device stopped working 30 minutes into the study. What is the next step in the management of this patient?
questions.solution: Correct Option A: In-lab polysomnography (PSG) This patient's presentation suggests obstructive sleep apnea (OSA). As per AASM guidelines, a patient with high suspicion of OSA and a negative HST should be evaluated with an in-lab PSG. False negatives are possible with home sleep testing due, in part, to the lack of EEG recording with most devices. The inability to score sleep requires the use of recording time rather than sleep time as the denominator in the AHI, which may result in an underestimation of AHI if the patient spends a significant amount of time awake during the study. The lack of EEG also precludes arousal scoring, which may result in decreased hypopnea scoring (if the event is terminated by an arousal and does not result in a 3-4% desaturation). In addition, technical issues may undermine the quality of the study. Home testing devices must be applied by the patient, and no technician is on-site to monitor the quality of the signals (as there is during a PSG). In this case, the loss of the oximetry signal may have resulted in a false negative. Without the ability to measure desaturations, only apneas (and not hypopneas) can be scored with this home study. Incorrect Options: Option B - No futher evaluation: The patient should undergo further testing to rule out OSA in the setting of a negative home test and high suspicion of OSA. Option C - Multiple sleep latency test (MSLT): An MSLT should only be performed for evaluation of sleepiness once significant OSA has been ruled out. Option D - Maintenance of wakefulness test (MWT): An MWT will not provide any diagnostic information on the cause of this patient’s sleepiness. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: A 25-year-old woman presents with acute-onset chest pain, difficulty breathing, and palpitations. Her history is only notable for an uncomplicated C-section delivery 2 weeks ago. She is not taking any medication other than occasional ibuprofen. Vital signs are blood pressure 125/68 mm Hg, heart rate 112 beats per minute, respiratory rate 22 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 98% on room air. The physical examination reveals a young woman in obvious pain and distress whenever she moves but is otherwise normal. ECG shows no acute ST changes, and cardiac biomarkers are negative. Chest radiograph is negative as well. Which of the following is the most appropriate pharmacologic therapy?
questions.stemHtml: A 25-year-old woman presents with acute-onset chest pain, difficulty breathing, and palpitations. Her history is only notable for an uncomplicated C-section delivery 2 weeks ago. She is not taking any medication other than occasional ibuprofen. Vital signs are blood pressure 125/68 mm Hg, heart rate 112 beats per minute, respiratory rate 22 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 98% on room air. The physical examination reveals a young woman in obvious pain and distress whenever she moves but is otherwise normal. ECG shows no acute ST changes, and cardiac biomarkers are negative. Chest radiograph is negative as well. Which of the following is the most appropriate pharmacologic therapy?
questions.solution: Correct Option B: Unfractionated heparin Systemic anticoagulation is the standard treatment for pulmonary embolism (PE). Although PE can have various clinical presentations, the index of suspicion is high when an otherwise-healthy patient presents with dyspnea, especially after recent surgery. The most common presenting symptom of PE is sudden-onset dyspnea that is unexplained by findings on a physical exam. Another common symptom is pleuritic chest pain. Vital signs may or may not be altered by the obstruction of flow caused by the embolism; for example, 50% of patients with demonstrated PE have a heart rate within normal limits. Diagnosis is made with Wells' criteria and confirmed with a helical CT. This patient's Wells' score is 6 (3 for alternative diagnosis less likely, 1.5 for surgery, and 1.5 for heart rate >100 bpm). In addition to UFH, LMWH or any of the direct oral anticoagulant agents (apixaban, dabigatran, rivaroxaban, or edoxaban) would also be appropriate for initial systemic anticoagulation. The decision about which anticoagulant to select is complex and should be based on clinical experience as well as bleeding risk, patient comorbidities, patient preference, cost, and convenience for the patient. Incorrect Options: Option A - Aspirin and nitroglycerin: Aspirin and nitroglycerin are the treatment for dyspnea due to MI. EKG results are often positive, and biomarkers are elevated. Option C - Lasix: Lasix is used in the treatment of dyspnea secondary to CHF, which usually presents with rales on lung exam or signs of pulmonary edema on CXR. Option D - Alteplase: Alteplase or tissue plasminogen is used to break down blood clots in severe PE presenting with hemodynamic compromise. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: A 5-year-old child presents with fever, sore throat, and a greyish-white pseudo membrane covering the tonsils and pharynx. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis in this patient?
questions.stemHtml: A 5-year-old child presents with fever, sore throat, and a greyish-white pseudo membrane covering the tonsils and pharynx. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis in this patient?
questions.solution: Correct Option B: Diphtheria Fever, sore throat, and a greyish-white pseudomembrane suggest a diagnosis of diphtheria. Corynebacterium diphtheriae is responsible for causing diphtheria. Spread of infection: The primary mode of transmission of diphtheria is person-to-person spread through respiratory droplets generated by coughing or sneezing. Clinical features of diphtheria: Sore throat Low-grade fever Malaise Weakness Swollen neck glands (lymph nodes) Pseudomembrane formation (greyish-white membrane covering the tonsils, pharynx, or nasal cavity) Complications: Myocarditis Airway obstruction Neuropathy Septicaemia Diagnosis: A throat culture or swab is taken from the affected area to test for Corynebacterium diphtheriae . Treatment: Isolate the patient in a separate room Diphtheria antitoxin Intramuscular penicillin G or intravenous erythromycin Incorrect Options: Option A: Epiglottitis Epiglottitis is a severe bacterial infection of the epiglottis caused by Haemophilus influenzae type B. Clinical features of epiglottitis include high fever, difficulty swallowing, difficulty breathing, drooling, and stridor. Children are more commonly affected than adults. An X-ray of the neck may show a swollen epiglottis, which appears as a " thumb sign " on lateral neck radiography. Option C: Streptococcal pharyngitis Streptococcal pharyngitis, also known as strep throat, is caused by group A Streptococcus. It is characterised by fever, sore throat, and swollen lymph nodes. A physical exam may reveal redness and swelling of the tonsils and pharynx, but there is no pseudomembrane formation. Amoxicillin is used to treat streptococcal pharyngitis. Option D: Herpangiana Herpangina is caused by coxsackie virus . It is characterised by fever, sore throat, and the formation of small, painful ulcers on the back of the throat and tonsils. It is most commonly seen in children under 10 years of age It is a self-limiting disease and undergoes spontaneous resolution. However, there is no pseudomembrane formation in herpangina. @Neet_pg_bot

Spread of infection:

  • Sore throat
  • Low-grade fever
  • Malaise
  • Weakness
  • Swollen neck glands (lymph nodes)

  • Airway obstruction
  • Neuropathy
  • Septicaemia

Diagnosis:

  • A throat culture or swab is taken from the affected area to test for Corynebacterium diphtheriae.

Treatment:

  • Isolate the patient in a separate room
  • Diphtheria antitoxin
  • Intramuscular penicillin G or intravenous erythromycin

options.label: C

questions.solution: Correct Option A: Bilateral renal artery stenosis Flash pulmonary edema (FPE) is a nonspecific clinical term used to describe a dramatic form of acute decompensated heart failure. Many common findings like heart failure, hypertension, coronary ischemia, valvular heart disease, and diastolic dysfunction are associated with acute decompensated heart failure as well as with FPE. Nevertheless, endothelial dysfunction (possibly secondary to excessive activity of the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system) impaired nitric oxide synthesis, increased endothelin levels, and/or excessive circulating catecholamines may cause excessive pulmonary capillary permeability and facilitate FPE formation. Renal artery stenosis (chiefly bilateral) is a common cause of FPE. Lack of diurnal variation in blood pressure and widened pulse pressure are additional risk factors for FPE. Incorrect Options: Option B - Unilateral renal artery stenosis: Although unilateral renal artery stenosis can be a cause, it is less likely than bilateral. Option C - Normal left ventricular end diastolic pressure (LVEDP): Regardless of its etiology, an acute increase of LVEDP is essential for the development of FPE. Option D - Decreased LVEDP: An acute increase of LVEDP is essential for the development of FPE. @Neet_pg_bot

Leptospirosis is a bacterial disease caused by the bacterium Leptospira interrogans . Routes of the spread of infection: Leptospirosis is typically transmitted to humans through exposure to water or soil contaminated with urine from infected animals , such as rats, dogs, cattle, or pigs. Clinical features of leptospirosis include: Mild leptospirosis: Fever Headache Myalgia Conjunctival suffusion (redness) Severe leptospirosis (Weil disease or enterohemorrhagic leptospirosis): Fever Hepatitis (jaundice and hepatomegaly) Acute kidney injury (oliguria and hematuria) Anaemia It may also involve the heart, CNS, and muscles. Diagnosis : The diagnosis of leptospirosis is confirmed with the help of a microscopic agglutination test. Treatment : Mild leptospirosis: Oral doxycycline or azithromycin. Severe leptospirosis: Intravenous penicillin, doxycycline, or ceftriaxone. Incorrect Options: Option A: Rocky Mountain spotted fever Rocky Mountain spotted fever is a bacterial disease caused by the bacterium Rickettsia rickettsii , which is transmitted by a Dermacentor tick bite . Symptoms may include fever, headache, muscle aches, and a maculopapular rash that starts on the ankles and wrists and spreads to the trunk, palm, and soles. However, it is not typically associated with jaundice or exposure to contaminated water. Option B: Legionellosis Legionellosis is a bacterial disease caused by the bacterium Legionella pneumophila . It is typically transmitted through exposure to contaminated water or air conditioning systems. Clinical features include fever, cough, muscle aches, diarrhoea, and hyponatremia. However, legionellosis is not typically associated with jaundice. Option C: Brucellosis Brucellosis is a bacterial disease caused by the bacterium Brucella . It is typically contracted through ingesting contaminated raw meat, unpasteurised mil k, or contact with infected animals. Symptoms may include fever, muscle aches, lymphadenopathy, and joint pain. However, brucellosis is not typically associated with jaundice or exposure to contaminated water. @Neet_pg_bot

The patient responded well to the procedure and was able to be weaned off ventilator support without issue. options.label: A
options.text: PCR of airways and surgical site for Mycobacterium hominis

options.label: D
options.text: Serum ammonia levels should be part of the routine lung transplant workup

questions.solution: Correct Option C: Initiation of hemodialysis Mycoplasma hominis is quite rare in lung transplants, and when combined with liver failure and urea cycle enzyme deficiencies comprise the 1-4% incidence of hyperammonemia observed in lung transplant patients, which may result in profound effects on the central nervous system. The initiation of hemodialysis in order to rapidly decrease the patient’s ammonia level and avoid further CNS complications would be the most appropriate action in this case due to the high mortality rate. Incorrect Options: Option A - PCR of airways and surgical site for Mycobacterium hominis: PCR of airways and surgical site for Mycobacterium hominis in the recipient in addition to PCR testing of the donor’s airways would be the appropriate action once the patient’s hyperammonemia and confusion are addressed. . Most cases of M. hominis are donor derived. Option B - Initiation of prophylactic antibiotic: The majority of prophylactic antibiotic regimens do not have coverage in place for Mycobacterium hominis, therefore culture with sensitivities and initiation of antibiotics which target M. hominis such as doxycycline, pending PCR results would be a more appropriate approach. Option D - Serum ammonia levels should be part of the routine lung transplant workup: It is more prudent to order serum ammonia levels if the patient exhibits signs of confusion, coma, seizures, or general lethargy which cannot be explained by another medical condition. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: A 33 year-old female is diagnosed with medullary thyroid cancer. Work-up reveals that she also has an underlying pheochromocytoma and parathyroid carcinoma. Which of the following familial endocrine neoplasia disorders does she likely have?
questions.stemHtml: A 33 year-old female is diagnosed with medullary thyroid cancer. Work-up reveals that she also has an underlying pheochromocytoma and parathyroid carcinoma. Which of the following familial endocrine neoplasia disorders does she likely have?
questions.solution: Correct Option B: MEN 2A MEN 2A (Multiple Endocrine Neoplasia type 2A): This syndrome is associated with medullary thyroid cancer, pheochromocytoma (a tumor of the adrenal glands that produces excess catecholamines), and primary hyperparathyroidism. Incorrect Options: Option A - MEN 1 (Multiple Endocrine Neoplasia type 1): This syndrome is characterized by tumors in three main endocrine glands - the parathyroid glands, the pancreas, and the pituitary gland. Tumors in the parathyroid glands can lead to primary hyperparathyroidism, while tumors in the pancreas can cause insulinomas (insulin-producing tumors) or gastrinomas (gastrin-producing tumors). Pituitary tumors can cause excess hormone production leading to various hormonal disorders. Option C - MEN 2B (Multiple Endocrine Neoplasia type 2B): This syndrome is also associated with medullary thyroid cancer and pheochromocytoma. Additionally, it is characterized by the development of neuromas (benign nerve tumors) on the lips, tongue, and gastrointestinal tract, as well as other distinctive features like marfanoid body habitus (long, slender limbs) and mucosal neuromas. It does not involve primary hyperparathyroidism. Option D - MEN 3 (Multiple Endocrine Neoplasia type 3), also known as MEN 2C: This syndrome is similar to MEN 2B and is associated with medullary thyroid cancer, pheochromocytoma, and neuromas, but does not involve primary hyperparathyroidism. @Neet_pg_bot

options.label: B
options.text: It is due to type 4 renal tubular acidosis

options.label: C
options.text: It is due to inadequate dialysis

options.label: D
options.text: It is due to her NPO status

questions.answerText: It is due to her NPO status
questions.solution: Correct Option D: It is due to her NPO status This patient has several reasons to have hyperkalemia. First of all, she has ESRD, making the renal removal of potassium minimal or non-existent. The fasting state is associate with a reductio of the circulating insulin levels, which in turn, will cause potassium to translocate from the intracellular to the extracellular space. The patient has a potassium source in the broken red blood cells in the gut and somatostatin decreased the insulin secretion, making it more difficult for the potassium to translocate back to the intracellular space. Also, the use of octreotide causes a further reduction in the insulin secretion. Incorrect Options: Option A - It is due to hyperinsulinemia: Unless severely malnourished, the fasting state is associated with hyperinsulinemia and hyperkalemia Option B - It is due to type 4 renal tubular acidosis: A patient with ESRD dose not have a significant number of functional renal tubules to cause type 4 renal tubular acidosis Option C - It is due to inadequate dialysis: In this case, the high BUN is most likely the consequence of the metabolism of amino acids in the liver. If the patient did not have cirrhosis, the BUN may even be higher @Neet_pg_bot

Correct Option D: It is due to her NPO status

The patient has a potassium source in the broken red blood cells in the gut and somatostatin decreased the insulin secretion, making it more difficult for the potassium to translocate back to the intracellular space. Also, the use of octreotide causes a further reduction in the insulin secretion.

Incorrect Options:

Option A - It is due to hyperinsulinemia: Unless severely malnourished, the fasting state is associated with hyperinsulinemia and hyperkalemia

Option B - It is due to type 4 renal tubular acidosis: A patient with ESRD dose not have a significant number of functional renal tubules to cause type 4 renal tubular acidosis

Option C - It is due to inadequate dialysis: In this case, the high BUN is most likely the consequence of the metabolism of amino acids in the liver. If the patient did not have cirrhosis, the BUN may even be higher

questions.solution: Correct Option B: Anti-double stranded DNA antibodies Since the introduction of anti-TNF agents, a new form of drug-induced lupus has been seen, anti-TNF-induced lupus. Its serological pattern is distinct in that anti dsDNA are present in the vast majority of cases. In classical drug-induced lupus, dsDNA is absent. The two main differential diagnoses are of "classical" drug-induced lupus which can be seen following treatment with minocycline or isoniazid, or anti-TNF induced lupus which tends to differ in terms of the serology. In anti-TNF induced lupus hypocomplementemia is much more frequent, and anti-dsDNA antibodies are present in ~90% of cases. In "classical" drug-induced lupus anti dsDNA antibodies are absent and hypocomplementemia is rarely seen. Antinuclear antibodies are present in both these conditions. His AFP level was normal and beta-hCG level was 488 IU/L. Based on the patient's clinical presentation, which of the following treatments would you recommend?
questions.stemHtml: A 28-year-old male who presented with mild chest pain, cough, and the subjective feeling of shortness of breath was evaluated, and found to have an anterior mediastinal mass with no additional lesion concerns for metastatic spread in his CT thorax. questions.solution: Correct Option D: Chemotherapy +/- surgery The patient's clinical presentation, including mild chest pain, cough, and subjective shortness of breath, along with the finding of an anterior mediastinal mass, raises suspicion for a nonseminomatous germ cell tumor (NSGCT) of the mediastinum. Additionally, the elevated beta-hCG level of 488 IU/L supports the diagnosis of a mediastinal NSGCT, as these tumors often produce elevated levels of beta-hCG. The management of mediastinal germ cell tumors involves a multimodal approach, including chemotherapy as the primary treatment. Chemotherapy is effective in treating both localized and metastatic disease. It aims to shrink the tumor and eliminate any micrometastases. Surgery may be considered after chemotherapy to resect any residual mass or to address localized disease. Incorrect Options: Option A - Surgery alone: Surgery alone is not the preferred initial treatment for mediastinal germ cell tumors. Chemotherapy is needed to target micrometastases and reduce tumor burden before considering surgery. Option B - Surgery + adjuvant chemotherapy: In the case of mediastinal germ cell tumors, chemotherapy is usually given as the primary treatment. Surgery may be considered after chemotherapy to address any remaining mass or localized disease. Adjuvant chemotherapy is not typically used in this scenario. Option C - Surgery + adjuvant radiation: While radiation therapy may have a role in the treatment of certain mediastinal tumors, it is not the primary treatment for mediastinal germ cell tumors. Chemotherapy is the mainstay of treatment, and surgery may be considered in selected cases. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: A 40-year-old female presents to the clinic with hemoptysis for 3 hours. She also complains of fatigue and low-grade fever. She further reports that she has darkened urine for the past couple of days. She has a history of serous otitis media. Laboratory results show positive c-ANCA. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.stemHtml: A 40-year-old female presents to the clinic with hemoptysis for 3 hours. She also complains of fatigue and low-grade fever. She further reports that she has darkened urine for the past couple of days. She has a history of serous otitis media. Laboratory results show positive c-ANCA. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.solution: Correct Option B: Granulomatous with polyangiitis This patient with otitis media, hemoptysis and dark urine along with positive c-ANCA most likely has Granulomatous with polyangiitis Features of Granulomatous with polyangiitis: Involvement of the upper airways occurs in 95% of patients with Wegener's polyangiitis. Patients frequently exhibit severe upper respiratory symptoms, including nasal mucosal ulcers, purulent or bloody nasal discharge, paranasal sinus discomfort and drainage, and more. Saddle nose deformity may result from a subsequent nasal septal perforation . A blocked eustachian tube might result in serous otitis media. In about 16% of patients, active illness or scarring causes subglottic tracheal stenosis, which can severely block the airway. Asymptomatic infiltrations or cough, hemoptysis, dyspnea, and chest tightness may be clinical manifestations of pulmonary involvement. 85 to 90 per cent of patients have it. Atelectasis with a blockage can develop from endobronchial illness, either in its active state or as a result of fibrous scarring. Involvement of the eyes (52%) can occur, which presents with scleritis, episcleritis and retroorbital mass. Papules, vesicles, palpable purpura, ulcers, or subcutaneous nodules are the most common skin lesions (46% of patients), and a biopsy reveals vasculitis. Renal disease is seen in 77% patients and is major cause of mortality in this disorder. It is evident that once clinically apparent renal functional impairment starts, fast progressive renal failure usually follows unless the proper therapy is begun, even though it may occasionally appear as a moderate glomerulitis with proteinuria, hematuria, and red blood cell casts. Other findings include raised ESR, anaemia, leukocytosis, elevated immunoglobulin especially IgA and elevated Rheumatoid factor. Antiproteinase-3 ANCA results are positive in about 90% of patients with active granulomatosis with polyangiitis (Wegener's). However, the sensitivity falls between 60 and 70 per cent when no active illness exists. Up to 20% may not exhibit ANCA. Incorrect Options: Option A: Goodpasture's syndrome Goodpasture's syndrome is characterized by hemoptysis and hematuria. c-ANCA is not positive in this condition. Moreover, upper respiratory involvement is not seen. Option C: Churg Strauss syndrome Churg-Strauss is also known as eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis, patients frequently have symptoms like fever, lethargy, anorexia, and weight loss. Other features include severe asthmatic attacks and pulmonary infiltrations. The second most frequent symptom is mono neuritis multiplex. Option D: Kawasaki disease Kawasaki disease is an acute, necrotizing vasculitis of unknown aetiology. Clinically, it is characterized by prolonged fever, non-exudative limbal sparing conjunctivitis, unilateral cervical lymphadenopathy, hand and feet oedema, and strawberry tongue. @Neet_pg_bot

  • It is associated with chronic Hep B infection and p-ANCA is negative in PAN
  • Lungs are sparred in PAN

Polyarteritis nodosa

  • Polyarteritis nodosa is a vasculitic disorder affecting medium-sized vessels including skin, GIT, kidneys, nerves, joints, and muscles, however, lungs are sparred
  • It is more common in males between 45-65 years of age
  • It is commonly associated with chronic Hep B infection. Vaccination against Hep B decreased the risk of incidence of this disease

    • Constitutional symptoms include fever, weight loss, malaise, arthralgia, and myalgia

      • Renal involvement is the most common: hypertension and may progress to renal insufficiency

      • Skin: rash and ulcerations
      • Polyneuropathy
      • GI: melena, abdominal pain, and vomiting
      • Lungs are sparred in PAN

Option A: Temporal arteritis

  • Temporal arteritis also known as giant cell arteritis can also give rise to raised ESR and CRP and constitutional symptoms however GCA typically manifests in women of age above 50 years

Option B: Takayasu arteritis

  • Takayasu arteritis can present with constitutional symptoms of fever, malaise, weight loss, and raised ESR and CRP
  • However, in Takayasu arteritis, there is inflammation of the aortic arch and its branches that manifests in females of age less than 4o as weak or absent peripheral pulses (pulseless disease), bilateral carotid bruit.

Option C: Microscopic polyangiitis

  • Microscopic polyangiitis causes inflammation of small arterioles that lead to RPGN that manifests as hematuria and hypertension and alveolar hemorrhage that manifests as hemoptysis
  • p-ANCA is positive in 70-80% of cases of microscopic polyangiitis

questions.stem: A 60 year old male c/c smoker presents to the ER with progressively worsening, position-dependent facial swelling, exacerbated in the supine position and are associated with bilateral neck and arm swelling, dizziness, nausea, vomiting, and dysphagia. CT thorax demonstrates a large, heterogeneous mediastinal mass involving the superior and middle mediastinum with its most superior aspect at the level of the inferior right thyroid gland and its most inferior aspect at the subcarinal region. The mass encompasses the paratracheal, precarinal and subcarinal regions and measures 10.7 x 7.0 x 11.4 cm and exerts mass effect on the right brachiocephalic vein and SVC, which are significantly narrowed and near completely occluded. There is also mass effect on the trachea which is deviated to the left. O/E, the patient is noted to have trouble breathing with stridor. What must be the next step in management for this patient?

questions.solution: Correct Option C: Emergent radiation oncology consultation to evaluate the patient for emergent radiation. The patient's symptoms, including progressively worsening, position-dependent facial swelling, bilateral neck and arm swelling, dizziness, nausea, vomiting, dysphagia, and stridor, are suggestive of superior vena cava (SVC) syndrome. The CT thorax findings of a large, heterogeneous mediastinal mass involving the superior and middle mediastinum, exerting mass effect on the right brachiocephalic vein and SVC, are consistent with SVC obstruction caused by the mediastinal mass. Superior vena cava syndrome is considered a medical emergency, and the patient requires urgent intervention. Radiation therapy is the treatment of choice for SVC syndrome caused by a mediastinal mass. It provides rapid relief of symptoms by shrinking the tumor and alleviating the obstruction of the SVC. It is not the appropriate next step in management. questions.solution: Correct Option A: Juvenile Dermatomyositis The most likely diagnosis in this case is Juvenile Dermatomyositis (JDM). JDM is a rare autoimmune disorder that primarily affects children and adolescents, characterized by muscle weakness and skin rash. The presence of polyarthralgia, difficulty mobilizing, periorbital edema, ulcerated rash over the extensor surfaces of several joints, and periungual telangiectasia are all suggestive of JDM. Laboratory investigations such as normal U&Es, negative rheumatoid factor, negative ANA, negative ENA, and normal HLA B27 and HLA B51 further support the diagnosis of JDM. Incorrect Options: Option B - Juvenile idiopathic arthritis (JIA): JIA is a group of chronic inflammatory joint diseases in children, but it does not typically present with periorbital edema, ulcerated rash, or periungual telangiectasia. Additionally, the negative rheumatoid factor and ANA in this case make JIA less likely. Option C - Kawasaki disease: Kawasaki disease is an acute febrile illness that primarily affects young children and is characterized by fever, mucocutaneous manifestations, and systemic inflammation. While it can cause arthritis-like symptoms, the absence of fever and other typical Kawasaki disease features make it an unlikely diagnosis. Option D - Systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE): SLE is an autoimmune connective tissue disorder that can cause arthritis and skin manifestations, but it typically involves multiple organs and systems. The absence of positive ANA and ENA, along with the specific clinical features seen in JDM, make SLE less likely. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.solution: Correct Option A: pembrolizumab 200mg every 3 weeks plus axitinib 5mg BID 4w on and 2w off Axitinib is a tyrosine kinase inhibitor (TKI) and is typically dosed orally at 5mg twice daily (BID). It is administered on a schedule of 4 weeks on and 2 weeks off. Pembrolizumab is an immune checkpoint inhibitor that targets PD-1. It is typically administered intravenously at a dose of 200mg every 3 weeks. In this case, the patient is receiving a combination of axitinib and pembrolizumab. The dosing schedule for pembrolizumab remains the same, which is 200mg every 3 weeks. For axitinib, it is given at a dose of 5mg BID but on a schedule of 4 weeks on and 2 weeks off. This means that the patient takes axitinib continuously for 4 weeks, followed by a 2-week break (off). KEYNOTE-426 trial showed a 90% 12-month OS with P+A vs P+Sunitinib. It combination has FDA approval. Option C - pembrolizumab 200mg every 3 weeks plus axitinib 5mg BID 4w on and 1w off: The schedule for axitinib in this option has a shorter break (1 week off) compared to the correct option (2 weeks off). questions.stem: A 47-year-old female presenting with right cheek swelling for 2 weeks is found to have right parotid gland swelling on physical examination. A Schirmer tear test is positive. Which of the following is least likely to be associated with this patient’s disease?
questions.stemHtml: A 47-year-old female presenting with right cheek swelling for 2 weeks is found to have right parotid gland swelling on physical examination. A Schirmer tear test is positive. Which of the following is least likely to be associated with this patient’s disease?
questions.solution: Correct Option D: Secondary sclerosing cholangitis The patient presents with parotid gland swelling, and a positive Schirmer test suggests a diagnosis of Sjogren syndrome. Sjogren syndrome is an autoimmune disorder characterised by lymphocytic infiltration of the salivary gland and lacrimal glands. This leads to glandular fibrosis and exocrine failure. It usually presents in females between 40-50 years of age . It may occur alone ( primary) or with other autoimmune diseases (secondary). The patients usually present with k eratoconjunctivitis sicca (due to lack of lubricating tears), conjunctivitis, blepharitis, keratitis, xerostomia, dental caries, salivary gland enlargement, Raynaud’s phenomenon, non-erosive arthritis, and fatigue. The other associated autoimmune diseases include: Systemic lupus erythematosus Primary biliary cirrhosis Progressive systemic sclerosis Myasthenia gravis Chronic active hepatitis Secondary sclerosing cholangitis is a chronic cholestatic biliary disease associated with inflammatory bowel disease . It has no relation with Sjogren syndrome. Incorrect Options: Option A: Myasthenia gravis Myasthenia gravis is an autoimmune disorder. It occurs due to antibodies against the postsynaptic acetylcholine receptor. It is associated with Sjogren syndrome. Option B: Progressive systemic sclerosis Progressive systemic sclerosis is a rheumatological disorder characterised by sclerodactyly, telangiectasias, calcinosis, Raynaud's phenomenon, and renal, pulmonary, gastrointestinal, and musculoskeletal manifestations. It is associated with Sjogren syndrome. Option C: Primary biliary cirrhosis Primary biliary cirrhosis is a chronic autoimmune condition in which the biliary ducts are destroyed. Anti-mitochondrial antibodies are positive. It is associated with Sjogren syndrome. @Neet_pg_bot

  • The patients usually present with keratoconjunctivitis sicca (due to lack of lubricating tears), conjunctivitis, blepharitis, keratitis, xerostomia, dental caries, salivary gland enlargement, Raynaud’s phenomenon, non-erosive arthritis, and fatigue.
  • The other associated autoimmune diseases include:
  • Systemic lupus erythematosus
  • Primary biliary cirrhosis
  • Progressive systemic sclerosis
  • Myasthenia gravis
  • Chronic active hepatitis
  • Secondary sclerosing cholangitis is a chronic cholestatic biliary disease associated with inflammatory bowel disease. It has no relation with Sjogren syndrome.

Option A: Myasthenia gravis

  • Myasthenia gravis is an autoimmune disorder.
  • It occurs due to antibodies against the postsynaptic acetylcholine receptor.
  • It is associated with Sjogren syndrome.

Option B: Progressive systemic sclerosis

  • Progressive systemic sclerosis is a rheumatological disorder characterised by sclerodactyly, telangiectasias, calcinosis, Raynaud's phenomenon, and renal, pulmonary, gastrointestinal, and musculoskeletal manifestations.
  • It is associated with Sjogren syndrome.

Option C: Primary biliary cirrhosis

  • Primary biliary cirrhosis is a chronic autoimmune condition in which the biliary ducts are destroyed.
  • Anti-mitochondrial antibodies are positive.
  • It is associated with Sjogren syndrome.

questions.stem: A 30-year-old female presents to the medical outpatient department due to painful swelling in her right hand for 2 months. The pain is present throughout the day, and she also complains of difficulty in performing her daily chores. On physical examination, the patient has swollen, red & tender DIP (distal interphalangeal joint) of the right hand. Nail pitting is also present on the right hand. She is HLA-B27 positive. What is the 1st line of management in this patient?
questions.stemHtml:
A 30-year-old female presents to the medical outpatient department due to painful swelling in her right hand for 2 months. The pain is present throughout the day, and she also complains of difficulty in performing her daily chores. On physical examination, the patient has swollen, red & tender DIP (distal interphalangeal joint) of the right hand. Nail pitting is also present on the right hand. She is HLA-B27 positive.
What is the 1st line of management in this patient?
questions.solution: Correct Option C: Non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs) This patient with painful swelling in the DIP joints of the right hand associated with skin findings has Psoriatic arthritis. The Initial management of psoriatic arthritis is with NSAIDS . NSAIDS are effective for joint symptoms and bone turnover but have no impact on skin lesions. NSAIDs should be given for the shortest period possible and at the lowest dose due to their potential toxicity in this high-risk population. They reversibly inhibit cyclooxygenase (both COX1 and COX2) and also blocks prostaglandin synthesis. They are used as antipyretics, analgesics, and anti-inflammatory agents. Adverse effects include gastric ulcers, renal ischaemia, interstitial nephritis, and aplastic anaemia. Incorrect Options: Option A - Corticosteroids: The patient is suffering from psoriatic arthritis, small doses of prednisolone with strict monitoring can be given and it may be given in the form of glucocorticoids injection, in case of severe pain but it’s not the 1 st line drug to treat psoriatic arthritis. Option B - Celecoxib: Celecoxib is a reversible and selective inhibitor of CO X-2 that, can be used in psoriatic arthritis but it is not as effective as NSAIDs for the relief of its symptoms. It is the preferred drug in the treatment of rheumatoid arthritis and osteoarthritis. Option D - Infliximab: Infliximab, a chimeric monoclonal antibody to TNF-α has also been shown to be effective in psoriatic arthritis, but again it is not the 1 st line drug due to its wide range of side effects. These agents have been shown to have a significant impact on most clinical manifestations, including skin and nails, peripheral and axial joints, enthesis, dactylitis, and also on some of the associated comorbidities such as cardiovascular disease. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: A 71-year-old male with metastatic prostate cancer presents to your clinic for routine follow up. He was diagnosed ~3 years ago with Gleason 5+5 = 10 adenocarcinoma of prostate, an initial PSA of 323.9 ng/mL, and thoracic and lumbar bony metastases, and was treated with ADT. He now presents with a PSA rise to 10.4 ng/ml and a total testosterone level of 5 ng/dL. You order a bone scan, which reveals new metastases in the pelvic bones, bilateral femurs, and ribs. You are concerned that the patient has developed castration-resistant prostate cancer. Which of the following is a mechanism of development of castration resistance?
questions.stemHtml: A 71-year-old male with metastatic prostate cancer presents to your clinic for routine follow up. He was diagnosed ~3 years ago with Gleason 5+5 = 10 adenocarcinoma of prostate, an initial PSA of 323.9 ng/mL, and thoracic and lumbar bony metastases, and was treated with ADT. He now presents with a PSA rise to 10.4 ng/ml and a total testosterone level of 5 ng/dL. You order a bone scan, which reveals new metastases in the pelvic bones, bilateral femurs, and ribs. You are concerned that the patient has developed castration-resistant prostate cancer. Which of the following is a mechanism of development of castration resistance?

options.label: B
options.text: Ligand independent activation of the androgen receptor, De novo synthesis of intratumoral androgens

options.label: C
options.text: Alterations in the androgen receptor (including splice variants)

questions.solution: Correct Option D: All of the above Castration-resistant prostate cancer (CRPC) is a stage of prostate cancer where the disease progresses despite androgen deprivation therapy (ADT). It is characterized by the cancer cells finding ways to survive and grow even in the absence of androgen stimulation. Multiple mechanisms contribute to the development of castration resistance, and they can occur independently or in combination. Option A - Androgen receptor up-regulation: In some cases of CRPC, the cancer cells may increase the expression of androgen receptors, making them more sensitive to the low levels of androgens that may still be present even after ADT. This heightened sensitivity allows the cancer cells to continue proliferating despite the decreased androgen levels. Option B - Ligand-independent activation of the androgen receptor: Cancer cells can develop mutations or alterations in the androgen receptor that allow it to become activated in the absence of androgens. This means that even when androgens are not present, the altered androgen receptor can continue to signal and promote tumor growth. De novo synthesis of intratumoral androgens: In CRPC, the tumor cells may acquire the ability to synthesize androgens within the tumor microenvironment. This allows them to sustain androgen receptor signaling even in the absence of circulating androgens, further promoting cancer cell growth. Option C - Alterations in the androgen receptor (including splice variants): The androgen receptor can undergo genetic changes, including the generation of splice variants. These variants may lack certain regions of the receptor, making them more active and resistant to ADT, leading to continued tumor growth. Incorrect Options: None of the options listed is incorrect. All of them are mechanisms involved in the development of castration-resistant prostate cancer. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: A 56-year old male diagnosed with a T2N2bM0 squamous cell carcinoma of the right tonsil, HPV+, and CT of the head and neck showing a well lateralized tonsillar lesion with styptic appearing lymph nodes in cervical levels 2/3, presents to your clinic. He gives history of having multiple sexual partners, prior to his marriage. You consider him in the low risk category according to the analysis performed in RTOG 0129 (Ang et al. NEJM 2010), a phase III randomized trial of locally advanced squamous cell carcinoma of the head and neck. Based on this classification what is his expected 3-year overall survival?
questions.stemHtml: A 56-year old male diagnosed with a T2N2bM0 squamous cell carcinoma of the right tonsil, HPV+, and CT of the head and neck showing a well lateralized tonsillar lesion with styptic appearing lymph nodes in cervical levels 2/3, presents to your clinic. He gives history of having multiple sexual partners, prior to his marriage. You consider him in the low risk category according to the analysis performed in RTOG 0129 (Ang et al. NEJM 2010), a phase III randomized trial of locally advanced squamous cell carcinoma of the head and neck. Based on this classification what is his expected 3-year overall survival?
questions.solution: Correct Option D : 93% Based on the patient's low-risk category his expected 3-year overall survival would be ~90%. For details about the study design and risk group classification, please see below. A thorough understanding of this trial is crucial for all medical oncologists. RTOG 0129 (Ang et al. NEJM 2010) was a phase III randomized controlled trial with an original intention to compare different radiation techniques with concurrent chemotherapy. Eligible patients included those with untreated stage III/IV squamous-cell carcinoma of the oropharynx, hypopharynx, or larynx without evidence of distant disease, Zubrod (ECOG) performance status of 0 or 1, and adequate bone marrow, hepatic, and renal function. Stratification was based on performance status, tumour site, and nodal status. Patients were than randomized into one of the following arms: Conventional fractionation with concurrent chemotherapy: Chemotherapy was cisplatin 100 mg/m2 days 1, 22, 43 (3 cycles). Accelerated fractionation with concurrent chemotherapy: Chemotherapy was cisplatin 100mg/m2 days 1, 22 (2 cycles). With a median follow-up of 4.8 years they reported the following: 3-year overall survival: 70.3% accelerated vs. 64.3% conventional p=0.18. There was also no significant difference in the two arms between progression free survival, patterns of failure, acute grade 3/4 toxicity, or late toxic events. More importantly, the authors performed a retrospective analysis of the association between tumor HPV status and survival among the patients enrolled in the study. questions.solution: Correct Option C: FIP1L1–PDGFRA The correct fusion protein formed as a result of del(4)(q12q12) is FIP1L1-PDGFRA. This fusion gene is associated with a subtype of eosinophilic leukemia known as FIP1L1-PDGFRA-positive chronic eosinophilic leukemia (CEL). Your OPD resident asks what is the medication to which the surgeon referred. Which of the following would be the most correct answer?
questions.stemHtml: A 72-year-old male with a recent diagnosis of metastatic melanoma, with a large nearly circumferential lesion on his right forearm with associated metastatic disease in the right axilla and right lung base is referred to your OPD , as, the surgeon recommends the use of Talimogene laherparepvec (T-VEC) as an initial first step in management. Your OPD resident asks what is the medication to which the surgeon referred. Which of the following would be the most correct answer?

options.label: A
options.text: Humanized IgG4 antibody that inhibits programmed death 1 (PD-1) receptor

options.label: B
options.text: Humanized IgG4 antibody that inhibits programmed death-ligand 1 (PD-L1)

options.label: C

questions.solution: Correct Option D: Genetically engineered oncolytic herpes virus Talimogene laherparepvec (T-VEC) is a genetically engineered oncolytic herpes virus that is approved for the treatment of metastatic melanoma. It is designed to selectively infect and replicate in cancer cells while sparing healthy cells. T-VEC carries the granulocyte-macrophage colony-stimulating factor (GM-CSF) gene, which stimulates the patient's immune system to attack the tumor. After the virus infects cancer cells, it causes their lysis (breakdown), releasing tumor antigens and GM-CSF. This process promotes an anti-tumor immune response, attracting immune cells to the tumor site and enhancing the destruction of cancer cells. Incorrect Options: Option A - Humanized IgG4 antibody that inhibits programmed death 1 (PD-1) receptor: This option refers to drugs like pembrolizumab and nivolumab, which are immune checkpoint inhibitors targeting the PD-1 receptor on T cells. By blocking the interaction between PD-1 and its ligands (PD-L1 and PD-L2), these drugs unleash the immune system to attack cancer cells. While PD-1 inhibitors have shown efficacy in melanoma treatment, they are different from T-VEC, which is an oncolytic virus therapy. Option B - Humanized IgG4 antibody that inhibits programmed death-ligand 1 (PD-L1): This option refers to drugs like atezolizumab and durvalumab, which are immune checkpoint inhibitors targeting the PD-L1 protein on cancer cells. By inhibiting PD-L1, these drugs prevent cancer cells from evading immune surveillance. However, they are not T-VEC, which is a genetically modified oncolytic virus therapy. Option C - Monoclonal antibody that binds to CTLA-4: This option refers to drugs like ipilimumab, an immune checkpoint inhibitor targeting CTLA-4. By blocking CTLA-4, ipilimumab enhances the activation of T cells, leading to an immune response against cancer cells. While ipilimumab is used in the treatment of melanoma, it is not T-VEC, which is a different type of therapy. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: A 55-year-old male, ECOG 0, presents with a recent diagnosis of DLBCL with an LDH level of 145 IU/L, and stage III disease. He has a low risk international prognostic index (IPI) score. He proceeds with gene expression profiling, and your colleague informs you that he is positive for a "double-hit" lymphoma. What is the diagnostic hallmark of “double-hit” lymphomas?
questions.stemHtml: A 55-year-old male, ECOG 0, presents with a recent diagnosis of DLBCL with an LDH level of 145 IU/L, and stage III disease. He has a low risk international prognostic index (IPI) score. He proceeds with gene expression profiling, and your colleague informs you that he is positive for a "double-hit" lymphoma. What is the diagnostic hallmark of “double-hit” lymphomas?

options.label: B
options.text: Translocation of c-MYC and either BCL-2 or BCL-6

options.label: C
options.text: Translocation of c-MYC and BCL-2 and BCL-6

options.label: D

questions.answerText: Translocation of c-MYC and either BCL-2 or BCL-6
questions.solution: Correct Option B:Translocation of c-MYC and either BCL-2 or BCL-6 The diagnostic hallmark of "double-hit" lymphomas is the presence of specific chromosomal translocations involving the c-MYC gene and either the BCL-2 or BCL-6 gene. These translocations lead to the abnormal fusion of the c-MYC gene with either BCL-2 or BCL-6, resulting in dysregulated expression of these oncogenes. This dysregulation plays a critical role in the pathogenesis of "double-hit" lymphomas, contributing to their aggressive behavior and poor prognosis. Incorrect Options: Option A - Over-expression of c-MYC and BCL-2: While over-expression of c-MYC and BCL-2 may occur in certain lymphomas, it is not the specific diagnostic hallmark of "double-hit" lymphomas. The key feature of "double-hit" lymphomas is the presence of translocations involving c-MYC and either BCL-2 or BCL-6, not just over-expression of these genes. Option C - Translocation of c-MYC and BCL-2 and BCL-6: This option incorrectly includes all three translocations (c-MYC, BCL-2, and BCL-6) as diagnostic hallmarks of "double-hit" lymphomas. The correct answer is B, which states that "double-hit" lymphomas have translocations involving c-MYC and either BCL-2 or BCL-6, but not necessarily all three. Option D - Extra copies/amplifications of the c-MYC and BCL-2 genes: While gene amplifications or extra copies of c-MYC and BCL-2 genes may be observed in certain lymphomas, they are not the specific diagnostic hallmark of "double-hit" lymphomas. The critical feature is the presence of translocations involving c-MYC and either BCL-2 or BCL-6 genes, leading to abnormal fusion proteins. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: A 27-year-old man with a f/h of unexplained thrombocytopenia as well as sensorineural deafness in father and brother, presents after a low impact auto accident and is found to have a large area of ecchymosis on his flank and persistent thrombocytopenia 42,000. The patient has a history of moderate mucocutaneous bleeding (after oral surgery) and sporadic nosebleeds that have required packing on occasion, but has never received platelet transfusion. Morphology review of his peripheral blood smear demonstrated the presence of giant platelets as well as basophilic inclusions within neutrophils. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.stemHtml:
A 27-year-old man with a f/h of unexplained thrombocytopenia as well as sensorineural deafness in father and brother, presents after a low impact auto accident and is found to have a large area of ecchymosis on his flank and persistent thrombocytopenia 42,000. The patient has a history of moderate mucocutaneous bleeding (after oral surgery) and sporadic nosebleeds that have required packing on occasion, but has never received platelet transfusion.
Morphology review of his peripheral blood smear demonstrated the presence of giant platelets as well as basophilic inclusions within neutrophils. Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.solution: Correct Option B: MYH9-related disease The most likely diagnosis in this case is MYH9-related disease (also known as May-Hegglin anomaly). MYH9-related disease is an autosomal dominant inherited disorder caused by mutations in the MYH9 gene, which encodes the non-muscle myosin heavy chain IIA (NMMHC-IIA). This gene is responsible for the formation of myosin, a protein involved in various cellular processes, including platelet function and cytoplasmic organization of cells. Clinical features of MYH9-related disease include: Thrombocytopenia: Patients with MYH9-related disease typically have mild to moderate thrombocytopenia, which is a decrease in platelet count. In this case, the patient's platelet count is 42,000/μL. Giant platelets: Peripheral blood smear examination reveals the presence of large platelets, known as giant platelets, which are a characteristic finding in MYH9-related disease. Neutrophil inclusions: Another characteristic feature of MYH9-related disease is the presence of basophilic inclusions within neutrophils, which are known as Döhle-like bodies. These clinical and laboratory findings help differentiate MYH9-related disease from other platelet disorders. Incorrect Options: Option A - Glanzmann thrombasthenia: It is a different inherited platelet disorder characterized by a deficiency or dysfunction of the GPIIb/IIIa complex on platelets. It leads to impaired platelet aggregation, causing a bleeding tendency. Glanzmann thrombasthenia does not involve giant platelets or neutrophil inclusions. Option C: Hermansky-Pudlak syndrome: It is a group of rare genetic disorders characterized by oculocutaneous albinism, bleeding diathesis, and other systemic complications. It is caused by mutations in various genes involved in vesicle formation and trafficking. Hermansky-Pudlak syndrome does not typically present with giant platelets or neutrophil inclusions. Option D: Scott syndrome: It is another rare inherited platelet disorder characterized by impaired platelet procoagulant activity. It involves defects in phospholipid scrambling, leading to defective coagulation responses. Scott syndrome does not involve giant platelets or neutrophil inclusions. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.answerText: Congestive heart failure with reduced ejection fraction
questions.solution: Correct Option D: Congestive heart failure with reduced ejection fraction The constellation of findings described in the patient's laboratory analysis, including low hemoglobin, elevated LDH, undetectable haptoglobin, elevated reticulocyte count, schistocytosis, and polychromasia, is indicative of hemolytic anemia with peripheral red blood cell destruction (hemolysis). This pattern is commonly seen in conditions like hemolytic-uremic syndrome, thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura, and other microangiopathic hemolytic anemias. Congestive heart failure (CHF) with reduced ejection fraction is not a well-recognized cause of hemolysis and the constellation of findings seen in microangiopathic hemolytic anemias. While CHF can lead to anemia due to decreased production of red blood cells (anemia of chronic disease), it is not typically associated with hemolysis and the characteristic peripheral blood smear findings of microangiopathic hemolytic anemia. This can lead to the constellation of findings described in microangiopathic hemolytic anemias. Option B - Systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE): SLE can cause autoimmune hemolytic anemia, where the immune system attacks and destroys red blood cells, leading to hemolysis. Which of the following drugs can be used to treat this patient’s symptoms?
questions.solution: Correct Option D: Steroids Systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) is an autoimmune disorder affecting multiple body organs, such as kidneys, joints, and skin. Diagnosis is made by proper history, physical examination, and laboratory tests. Antinuclear antibodies (ANA) levels are measured if there is suspicion of SLE. It is conducted to screen SLE, and if it comes positive, anti-double stranded DNA antibodies serologic testing should be performed to confirm the diagnosis of SLE. Unfortunately , there is no cure for SLE. However, several medications can be used to control the symptoms of SLE. Hydroxychloroquine is the corner stone of the treatment of SLE, regardless of the disease severity. Mild to moderate symptoms of SLE can be treated with NSAIDs or hydroxychloroquine. However , steroids like prednisone are usually usedwith or without other immunosuppressants to achieve remission. High doses of steroids like methylprednisolone are usually prescribed to control severe diseases such as the involvement of kidneys and the brain. Steroids counter inflammation in individuals with SLE and decrease the severity of disease. Common steroids used in SLE include prednisone, prednisolone, hydrocortisone, dexamethasone, and triamcinolone. Common side effects of corticosteroids include weight gain, bruises, osteoporosis, diabetes, and increased risk of infection. Incorrect Options: Option A: Paracetamol Paracetamol is recommended for mild pain , such as tension headaches. It is also used as an antipyretic . Corticosteroids should be prescribed to this patient to decrease inflammatory reactions. Option B: Proton-pump inhibitors Proton pump inhibitors (PPI) decrease acid production in the stomach. These drugs inhibit the H+/K+ ATPase proton pump. These medications can be used for medical conditions like dyspepsia, peptic ulcer, gastroesophageal reflux disease, and Barrett's oesophagus. This patient should be given corticosteroids to control the symptoms of SLE. Option C: Opioids Opioids belong to the type of medication that is used to alleviate pain. It is prescribed to reduce moderate to severe pain and serious side effects. Corticosteroids are indicated in this patient to control the symptoms of SLE. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stemHtml: A 59-year-old female who presented to her gynaecologist with postcoital bleeding, of 3 months duration, on examination, was found to have a 3 x 3 cm mass in the distal left aspect of the vaginal canal. The lesion was biopsied and found to be consistent with adenocarcinoma (clear cell variant). Which of the following is a strong risk factor for the development of this malignancy?
questions.solution: Correct Option B: Maternal exposure to diethylstilbestrol (DES) Maternal exposure to diethylstilbestrol (DES) is a strong risk factor for the development of clear cell adenocarcinoma of the vagina. DES is a synthetic estrogen that was prescribed to pregnant women from the 1940s to the early 1970s to prevent miscarriages and other pregnancy complications. Unfortunately, it was later discovered that DES exposure in the womb could lead to various health issues in female offspring, including the rare occurrence of clear cell adenocarcinoma of the vagina. The risk is especially high for women whose mothers received DES during pregnancy. Incorrect Options: Option A - Nulliparity until age 40: Nulliparity (never having given birth) until age 40 is not specifically associated with an increased risk of clear cell adenocarcinoma of the vagina. However, it is essential to consider that certain risk factors for gynecological malignancies may involve reproductive history, and regular gynecological examinations are recommended for early detection. Option C - Obesity with a BMI >35: Obesity is a risk factor for several cancers, but there is no direct evidence linking it to an increased risk of clear cell adenocarcinoma of the vagina. Option D - Hypertension along with hyperlipidemia: Hypertension and hyperlipidemia are not known to be specific risk factors for clear cell adenocarcinoma of the vagina. @Neet_pg_bot
