questions.solution: Correct Option A: Presence of 4 or more out of 11 criteria The diagnosis of SLE is based on a combination of clinical and laboratory features. To be diagnosed with SLE, a patient must have at least 4 of the following 11 criteria: Malar rash : a permanent erythema across the malar eminences, either flat or elevated, with a propensity to sparing the nasolabial folds Discoid rash : erythematous elevated patches with follicular clogging and adherent keratotic scaling Photosensitivity: skin rash brought on by an unusual UV sensitivity Oral ulcers : Usually painless, oral or nasopharyngeal ulcers Arthritis : nonerosive arthritis characterised by discomfort, swelling, or effusion that affects two or more peripheral joints Serositis: pericarditis or pleuritis Renal disorder : cellular casts or elevated protein levels in urine (>0.5 g/day) Neurologic disorder : psychosis or seizures Haematologic disorder : anaemia (haemolytic in nature), decreased WBCs (<4,000/mm³) or lymphopenia (<1,500/mm³) or decreased platelets (<100,000/mm³) Immunologic disorder : positive anti-dsDNA or anti-Sm or antiphospholipid antibody or false-positive syphilis test Positive antinuclear antibody (ANA) test. Incorrect Options: Option B: Positive antinuclear antibodies and presence of rash Positive antinuclear antibodies are sensitive but not specific to diagnosing SLE. The presence of ANA and rash are suggestive of SLE; however, the patient must meet at least 4 criteria, and rash alone is not sufficient for a diagnosis of SLE. Option C: Positive antinuclear antibodies and presence of arthritis Positive antinuclear antibodies are sensitive but not specific to diagnosing SLE. The presence of ANA and arthritis are suggestive of arthritis; however, only one of the 11 criteria and does not fulfil the requirement for a diagnosis of SLE. Option D: Positive antinuclear antibodies and presence of renal involvement Positive antinuclear antibodies are sensitive but not specific to diagnose SLE. The presence of ANA and renal involvement are suggestive of the disease because renal involvement is only one of the 11 criteria, and the patient must meet at least 4 of these criteria for a diagnosis of SLE. @Neet_pg_bot
questions.solutionHtml:
Correct Option A: Presence of 4 or more out of 11 criteria

  • The diagnosis of SLE is based on a combination of clinical and laboratory features. To be diagnosed with SLE, a patient must have at least 4 of the following 11 criteria:
    • Malar rash: a permanent erythema across the malar eminences, either flat or elevated, with a propensity to sparing the nasolabial folds
    • Discoid rash: erythematous elevated patches with follicular clogging and adherent keratotic scaling
    • Photosensitivity: skin rash brought on by an unusual UV sensitivity
    • Oral ulcers: Usually painless, oral or nasopharyngeal ulcers
    • Arthritis: nonerosive arthritis characterised by discomfort, swelling, or effusion that affects two or more peripheral joints
    • Serositis: pericarditis or pleuritis
    • Renal disorder: cellular casts or elevated protein levels in urine (>0.5 g/day)
    • Neurologic disorder: psychosis or seizures
    • Haematologic disorder: anaemia (haemolytic in nature), decreased WBCs (<4,000/mm³) or lymphopenia (<1,500/mm³) or decreased platelets (<100,000/mm³)
    • Immunologic disorder: positive anti-dsDNA or anti-Sm or antiphospholipid antibody or false-positive syphilis test
    • Positive antinuclear antibody (ANA) test.


Incorrect Options: 

Option B: Positive antinuclear antibodies and presence of rash

  • Positive antinuclear antibodies are sensitive but not specific to diagnosing SLE. The presence of ANA and rash are suggestive of SLE; however, the patient must meet at least 4 criteria, and rash alone is not sufficient for a diagnosis of SLE.

Option C: Positive antinuclear antibodies and presence of arthritis

  • Positive antinuclear antibodies are sensitive but not specific to diagnosing SLE. The presence of ANA and arthritis are suggestive of arthritis; however, only one of the 11 criteria and does not fulfil the requirement for a diagnosis of SLE.

Option D: Positive antinuclear antibodies and presence of renal involvement

  • Positive antinuclear antibodies are sensitive but not specific to diagnose SLE. The presence of ANA and renal involvement are suggestive of the disease because renal involvement is only one of the 11 criteria, and the patient must meet at least 4 of these criteria for a diagnosis of SLE.

questions.stem: A 55-year-old Caucasian female presented in OPD for her generalised checkup as her history of rheumatoid arthritis has been positive for the last 6 years. She reported a history of pain and stiffness in small joints of the hand, including metacarpophalangeal and proximal interphalangeal joints, and significant weight loss. Skin pigmentation and rheumatoid nodules over the extensor tendons are present on examination. A physician further noted the presence of splenomegaly. Her lab reports showed neutropenia and thrombocytopenia. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.stemHtml: A 55-year-old Caucasian female presented in OPD for her generalised checkup as her history of rheumatoid arthritis has been positive for the last 6 years. She reported a history of pain and stiffness in small joints of the hand, including metacarpophalangeal and proximal interphalangeal joints, and significant weight loss. Skin pigmentation and rheumatoid nodules over the extensor tendons are present on examination. A physician further noted the presence of splenomegaly. Her lab reports showed neutropenia and thrombocytopenia. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.solution: Correct Option A: Felty's syndrome Felty's syndrome is a rare complication of seropositive RA in which splenomegaly occurs in combination with neutropenia and thrombocytopenia . Felty's syndrome occurs in patients with long-standing rheumatoid arthritis. The age of onset is mostly 50-70 years, with increased incidence in females compared to males ( particularly Caucasian> black females ). Localised or generalised lymphadenopathy can occur in patients with active disease. Other common clinical features are keratoconjunctivitis sicca, vasculitis, leg ulcers, recurrent infections and nodules. Laboratory findings include normochromic normocytic anaemia, neutropenia, thrombocytopenia, impaired T and B cell immunity and abnormal liver function. It also includes seropositive for rheumatoid factor. Other clinical findings may include multiple organs causing pleuritis, peripheral neuropathy, episcleritis, and signs of portal hypertension. Complications of felty's syndrome include splenic rupture, life-threatening infection and GI bleeding due to portal hypertension. Incorrect Options: Option B: Caplan syndrome It presents lung involvement along with clinical features of rheumatoid arthritis. It involves rheumatoid pneumoconiosis. Option C: Gouty arthritis Gouty arthritis is associated with the deposition of needle-like uric acid crystals in a joint resulting in inflammatory attacks. Option D: Systemic sclerosis It is an autoimmune group of diseases that involve the tightening and hardening of skin along with the involvement of internal organs @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: A 29-year-old Indian female presents to the outpatient clinic complaining of lower back pain. It started four months ago and has been persistent. She has taken acetaminophen but has not found any relief. She has a history of Crohn's disease. A treatment plan is made after a discussion with the patient. She agrees to start infliximab. Which of the following investigations is necessary before this patient can be started on infliximab?
questions.stemHtml: A 29-year-old Indian female presents to the outpatient clinic complaining of lower back pain. It started four months ago and has been persistent. She has taken acetaminophen but has not found any relief. She has a history of Crohn's disease. A treatment plan is made after a discussion with the patient. She agrees to start infliximab. Which of the following investigations is necessary before this patient can be started on infliximab?
questions.solution: Correct Option D: Interferon Gamma Release Assay (IGRA) IGRA is a blood test used to diagnose latent or active tuberculosis. When leukocytes are exposed to antigens of Mycobacterium tuberculosis, they release IG. IGRA measures the amount of IG released by leukocytes. This test is necessary because if a patient with latent tuberculosis is given infliximab, they will develop reactivation of tuberculosis. This patient is a resident of a country where tuberculosis is endemic. This further stresses the importance of IGRA. In some cases, the reactivation may be severe and progress to miliary tuberculosis. Regardless of the underlying disease process, screening all patients for latent tuberculosis before initiating infliximab is recommended. Incorrect Options: Option A - Complete Blood Count: A complete blood count (CBC) is not a necessary screening test for patients about to be started on infliximab. Although infliximab can rarely cause aplastic anaemia, a screening CBC is unlikely to be of any benefit. Option B - Serum creatinine: Biologic disease-modifying antirheumatic drugs (DMARDs) are technically antibodies. The degradation of antibodies is carried out by the reticuloendothelial system, not the liver or the kidney. Furthermore, infliximab is not associated with renal failure. Option C - Serum alanine transaminase: Biologic disease-modifying antirheumatic drugs (DMARDs) are technically antibodies. The degradation of antibodies is carried out by the reticuloendothelial system, not the liver or the kidney. Furthermore, infliximab is not associated with liver failure unless a patient has chronic hepatitis due to a viral infection. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.solution: Correct Option C: Induction therapy with ATRA plus anthracycline-based chemotherapy followed by consolidation therapy with two cycles of consolidation therapy with ATO, followed by two cycles of daunorubicin plus ATRA The patient's presentation with easy fatigability, bruises, and bleeding along with laboratory findings of low hemoglobin (7.8 g/dL) and extremely low platelet count (13,000/μL) is suggestive of acute promyelocytic leukemia (APL). The identification of the PML-RARA fusion gene confirms the diagnosis of APL. APL is a disease that belongs to the broader disease category of acute leukemias and is a clinically distinct disease process from Acute myeloid leukemia (AML). It is characterized by the presence of the PML-RARA fusion gene, which results from a reciprocal translocation between the PML gene on chromosome 15 and the RARA gene on chromosome 17. This fusion gene leads to the abnormal proliferation of promyelocytes in the bone marrow. The recommended treatment for APL is induction therapy with a combination of all-trans retinoic acid (ATRA) and anthracycline-based chemotherapy. ATRA is a vitamin A derivative that induces differentiation of the leukemic promyelocytes, while anthracycline-based chemotherapy helps in achieving remission. In The induction therapy with ATRA plus anthracycline-based chemotherapy, Following induction, consolidation therapy is given with two cycles of arsenic trioxide (ATO), which is highly effective in treating APL. After ATO consolidation, the patient receives two cycles of daunorubicin plus ATRA. This treatment approach has shown excellent outcomes in the management of APL and is currently considered the standard of care. Incorrect Options: Option A - Induction therapy with cytarabine (seven day continuous infusion) + an anthracycline (given days 1-3) (7+3 therapy) followed by allogenic hematopoietic cell transplantation (HCT): involve induction therapy with 7+3 therapy, which is the standard induction regimen for non-APL AML and not appropriate for APL. On examination, there is tenderness and swelling of both wrist joints and MCP joints sparring the DIP joints, and subcutaneous nodules on the extensor surface of the forearms that are mobile and firm. Which of the following is the most appropriate therapy for the acute presentation of this patient?
questions.stemHtml: A 40-year-old female presented in the emergency department with complaints of severe pain in her fingers and both wrist joints for 1-day. She gives a history of similar episodes of pain in the joints associated with stiffness in joints that persist for 90 minutes after she wakes up in the morning. She is vitally stable. On examination, there is tenderness and swelling of both wrist joints and MCP joints sparring the DIP joints, and subcutaneous nodules on the extensor surface of the forearms that are mobile and firm. Which of the following is the most appropriate therapy for the acute presentation of this patient?
questions.solution: Correct Option D: Prednisolone This patient has classical features of rheumatoid arthritis that include symmetrical involvement of small joints ( MCP and PIP joints) and sparring DIP joints , morning stiffness, and rheumatoid nodules on the extensor surfaces Worsening symptoms for the last day are indicative of an acute flare of disease The treatment of choice for acute flares of rheumatoid arthritis is prednisolone Management of acute flare of rheumatoid arthritis The drugs that are used for the symptomatic relief of RA are anti-inflammatory drugs i.e glucocorticoids (prednisolone) and NSAIDs. Glucocorticoids therapy is more effective than NSAIDs for the rapid reduction of the severity of symptoms like joint pain and tenderness Glucocorticoids can be administered via systemic route or intramuscular injections Long-term therapy with glucocorticoids has many adverse effects like hypertension, diabetes mellitus, osteoporosis, etc therefore, glucocorticoids should be administered for a short term (less than 3 months) at the lowest effective dose Incorrect Options: Option A: Methotrexate Methotrexate is the first line DMARDs used for the treatment of RA Once RA is diagnosed, MTX should be initiated as soon as possible as it prevents progressive joint destruction in these patients However, the onset of action of MTX is weeks to months therefore, it can’t be used for the management of acute flares of RA Option B: Colchicine Colchicine is used for the treatment of acute gout Acute gout can also present with acute onset of joint pain and tenderness but it mostly affects a single joint (usually the knee joint, first metatarsophalangeal joint, or thumb) Option C: Adalimumab Adalimumab is a biologic DMARD used for the treatment of rheumatoid arthritis Adalimumab is introduced in the long-term therapy of RA, in patients who still have moderate or severe disease after 3 months of therapy with DMARDs (refractory RA) It should not be used as an initial therapy for RA and in acute flares of RA @Neet_pg_bot

questions.solution: Correct Option A: Dilatation of coronary vessels Dipyridamole is a phosphodiesterase type 3 inhibitor used for treating coronary stent restenosis and intermittent vascular claudication and as an antiplatelet (anti-angina, TIA/stroke prevention) drug. Dipyridamole induces coronary vasodilation by raising adenosine levels and activating adenosine A2A receptors . Myocardial ischemia brought on by a shift of blood flow is known as coronary steal syndrome. The seriously stenotic arteries rigidity only permits a small coronary flow reserve. Blood is therefore directed to collaterals and healthy vessels when coronary arteries widen. As a result, there is tissue ischemia distal to the coronary artery stenosis , which causes chest tightness and novel ECG abnormalities. The adenosine or dipyridamole pharmacological stress test is based on this occurrence. questions.stem: A 31-year-old man came to the office with complaints of fever, dyspnea and chest pain on exertion. He had an upper respiratory tract infection 10 days back, which resolved spontaneously. His temperature is 100.4°F, blood pressure is 100/60 mmHg, heart rate is 110 bpm, and respiratory rate is 22/min. On examination, there is pedal oedema, S3 is audible and pulmonary crackles are heard in both lung fields. Which of the following is the most appropriate diagnostic test for this patient?
questions.stemHtml: A 31-year-old man came to the office with complaints of fever, dyspnea and chest pain on exertion. He had an upper respiratory tract infection 10 days back, which resolved spontaneously. His temperature is 100.4°F, blood pressure is 100/60 mmHg, heart rate is 110 bpm, and respiratory rate is 22/min. On examination, there is pedal oedema, S3 is audible and pulmonary crackles are heard in both lung fields. Which of the following is the most appropriate diagnostic test for this patient?
questions.solution: Correct Option C: Echocardiography This patient has developed fever, tachycardia, tachypnea, hypotension, an audible S3 and pulmonary crackles after an upper respiratory tract infection, indicating that he has developed viral myocarditis. Viral myocarditis is an inflammatory process of the myocardium. It can result in either focal or diffuse involvement of the myocardium. The viral infection is the most common underlying etiology, i.e. coxsackie virus, Parvo B-19 virus and HPV-6 virus, being the main culprits. Other causes include rheumatic heart disease, chagas disease, and SLE. The patients usually have a 1 to 2-week history of flu-like illness, i.e. fever, malaise, and myalgias which progress to dyspnea and chest pain on exertion. There is audible S3, hypotension and dependent oedema on examination. The diagnosis is usually made on clinical presentation, and invasive imaging is rarely required. Echocardiography is usually done to check the heart's functioning and the disease's severity. There will be reduced left ventricular function, global hypokinesis, and regional wall motion abnormalities on echo. Incorrect Options: Option A - Endomyocardial biopsy : It is the gold standard test to diagnose myocarditis; however, it is rarely used because it is an invasive test , and the diagnosis is usually made on clinical presentation. Option B - Electrocardiography : It can be obtained in patients with myocarditis, and findings can include sinus tachycardia, widened QRS patterns, low voltage, prolonged QT, and variable atrioventricular (AV) blocks . Option D - CT angiography : It is done to diagnose the pulmonary embolism , which can present with hypotension, tachycardia, and tachypnea; however, there will be no S3, and the lungs are clear on auscultation. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: A 21-year-old man presents in the medical emergency room with dyspnea, abdominal distension and bilateral pedal swellings from the last 1 week. It is associated with a preceding one-month history of weight loss, fever and anorexia. On physical examination, his blood pressure is 70/40 mmHg, heart rate is 109/min, respiratory rate is 28/min, and temperature is 101°F. He has raised JVP, which falls paradoxically in inspiration. A precordial auscultation reveals muffled heart sounds. A pulsus paradoxus is present. A chest x-ray shows cardiomegaly with right apical consolidation. Considering the likely diagnosis, what is the best management of this patient's presentation?

It is associated with a preceding one-month history of weight loss, fever and anorexia. On physical examination, his blood pressure is 70/40 mmHg, heart rate is 109/min, respiratory rate is 28/min, and temperature is 101°F. He has raised JVP, which falls paradoxically in inspiration. A precordial auscultation reveals muffled heart sounds. A pulsus paradoxus is present. A chest x-ray shows cardiomegaly with right apical consolidation. Considering the likely diagnosis, what is the best management of this patient's presentation?
questions.solution: Correct Option B: Therapeutic pericardiocentesis and antituberculous treatment The underlying diagnosis here is tuberculous effusive-pericarditis with massive pericardial effusion causing cardiac tamponade . Urgent therapeutic pericardiocentesis and starting timely initiation of antituberculous treatment is the best treatment option. Secondary localization of mycobacterium tuberculosis in the pericardium from a primary infection produces tuberculous pericarditis, especially in countries with high TB prevalence. It may present as constrictive pericarditis, isolated pericardial effusion or effusive-constrictive pericarditis. The primary infection in this patient is likely the right lung apex, as suggested by a chest X-ray. For a definitive diagnosis of tuberculous pericarditis, tubercle bacilli should be demonstrated in the pericardial tissue of fluid. Supportive evidence includes a lymphocytic exudative pericardial effusion with elevated adenosine deaminase (ADA) levels. Treatment includes urgent therapeutic pericardiocentesis in cases of impending pericardial tamponade, followed by a definite treatment with rifampicin, isoniazid, ethambutol, and pyrazinamide for at least 2 months which is followed by rifampicin and isoniazid for a total of 6 months. Adjunctive therapy with prednisolone for 6 weeks and intrapericardial injection of urokinase prevents a common complication of tuberculous pericarditis and constrictive pericarditis. A pericardiectomy is indicated when the patient's condition keeps deteriorating after 4-8 weeks of therapy. Incorrect Options: Option A - Start antituberculous treatment: Although antituberculous treatment should be started, this patient is in a hemodynamically unstable cardiac tamponade , which should be dealt with first. Management of vital signs is essential before starting the definite treatment. Antituberculous treatment should be started as soon as cardiac tamponade is relieved and the patient maintains vital signs. Option C - Therapeutic pericardiocentesis and NSAIDs: Although therapeutic pericardiocentesis should be done immediately, NSAIDs are not recommended to treat tuberculous effusive-pericarditis . NSAIDs are the treatment of choice for viral or idiopathic pericarditis with or without pericardial effusion. Option D - Therapeutic pericardiocentesis and prednisolone: Although therapeutic pericardiocentesis should be done immediately, prednisolone is not the definitive treatment for tuberculous pericarditis. Prednisolone, however, is used as an adjunctive treatment for tuberculous pericarditis. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stemHtml: A 60-year-old male patient came to the outpatient department with a complaint of pain in the right leg with prolonged walking for the last 2 months. There was intermittent claudication on walking. After an appropriate assessment, chronic limb ischaemia was diagnosed. A drug was prescribed with inhibiting activity against the PDE III enzyme. Which of the following is the drug given to this patient?
questions.solution: Correct Option D: Cilostazol This patient is suffering from chronic limb ischaemia in which there is a chronic diminished supply to blood of the affected limbs. The patients suffer from intermittent claudication, which is the production of pain on prolonged walking. It is due to an atherosclerotic plaque in the blood vessel which causes a reduction in meeting the demand of blood that is required during walking or exercising. One of the pharmacological a gents that is used for the treatment of chronic limb ischaemia is cilostazol. The mechanism of action of cilostazol is the inhibition of PDE III enzyme leading to an increase in cAMP. The increased cAMP results in an antiplatelet effect and also results in vasodilation by the action of increased cAMP in blood vessels. Other drugs include aspirin and statins. Incorrect Options: Option A - Aspirin: Aspirin is also used for the treatment of ischaemic limb disease. Aspirin prevents the formation of thrombosis and thus also prevents the progression of thrombus. The mechanism of action of aspirin is the inhibition of cyclooxygenase (COX) which normally produces prostaglandins . As a result, aspirin is used because of its antiplatelet effect. Option B - Acetaminophen: Acetaminophen is used for pain and fever management. It works by th e inhibition of cyclooxygenase enzymes in the CNS system. Acetaminophen does not have any antiplatelet effect which is why it is not used for the management of ischaemic limb disease. Option C - NSAID: NSAIDs work by inhibiting cyclooxygenase enzymes in CNS and peripheral systems. It is used as an anti-inflammatory, analgesic, and antipyretic. It is used for the management of chronic limb ischaemia. Some of the NSAIDs are ibuprofen, diclofenac, ketorolac, etc. Some of the side effects are gastric ulcers and NSAID-induced nephropathy. @Neet_pg_bot

The patient has a history of vascular claudication, diabetes, and hypertension. His current medications include atorvastatin, lisinopril, insulin, and metformin. He is vitally stable except his pulse rate is 140 beats per minute, and Oxygen saturation is 95% on room air. Basic laboratory values are ordered, as well as an initial set of cardiac troponins. An ECG is obtained which shows atrial fibrillation. Which of the following is the most appropriate long-term management to prevent thromboembolism for this patient's condition?
questions.solution: Correct Option C: Warfarin This patient is presenting with an ECG suggestive of atrial fibrillation. The best long-term management of this condition is warfarin . Atrial fibrillation can present with anxiety, a sensation of flutter in one's chest, and shortness of breath. Incorrect Options: Option B - Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy: Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy is a condition in which the heart muscle becomes abnormally thick, which can also lead to difficulty pumping blood effectively. However, patients with hypertrophic cardiomyopathy typically present with symptoms such as chest pain, palpitations, and syncope rather than exertional dyspnea and lower extremity oedema present in this patient. Option C - Restrictive cardiomyopathy: Restrictive cardiomyopathy is when the heart muscle becomes stiff and less compliant , leading to symptoms similar to dilated cardiomyopathy. However, patients with restrictive cardiomyopathy typically do not have an enlarged heart, and physical exam findings such as jugular venous distention and an S3 gallop are less common. Option D - Arrhythmogenic right ventricular cardiomyopathy: Arrhythmogenic right ventricular cardiomyopathy is a rare condition in which the heart muscle becomes replaced by fibrous and fatty tissue, leading to abnormal heart rhythms and possible sudden cardiac death. questions.stem: A 59-year-old man was admitted to the emergency department with diaphoresis and chest pain radiating to his left arm and jaw. He was diagnosed with an ST-segment elevation myocardial infarction (STEMI) and was treated with thrombolytic therapy. However, he developed severe shortness of breath and hypotension five days later. A harsh holosystolic murmur is heard at the left lower sternal border on auscultation, accompanied by a thrill. There is an increase in oxygen saturation in the right ventricle compared to the right atrium on right heart catheterisation. Efforts are made to resuscitate the patient, but he collapses. What is the likely complication that patient is experiencing after his myocardial infarction?
questions.stemHtml: A 59-year-old man was admitted to the emergency department with diaphoresis and chest pain radiating to his left arm and jaw. He was diagnosed with an ST-segment elevation myocardial infarction (STEMI) and was treated with thrombolytic therapy. However, he developed severe shortness of breath and hypotension five days later. A harsh holosystolic murmur is heard at the left lower sternal border on auscultation, accompanied by a thrill. There is an increase in oxygen saturation in the right ventricle compared to the right atrium on right heart catheterisation. Efforts are made to resuscitate the patient, but he collapses. What is the likely complication that patient is experiencing after his myocardial infarction?
questions.solution: Correct Option B: Interventricular septum rupture An interventricular septum rupture (IVSR) is a rare but serious complication that can occur after a myocardial infarction (heart attack). The rupture typically occurs within the first week after myocardial infarction. It occurs when the infarcted tissue in the interventricular septum ruptures, leading to the development of a left-to-right shunt which often presents as right heart failure or as biventricular failure. The symptoms of an IVSR can include shortness of breath, severe hypotension and sometimes chest pain. These symptoms can be severe and quickly worsen, leading to cardiogenic shock. It causes a harsh murmur at the lower left sternal border , radiating to the right sternal border. The diagnosis is confirmed by Doppler echocardiography and right heart catheterisation . On right heart catheterisation, there is an increase in oxygen saturation in the right ventricle compared to the right atrium due to the presence of a shunt. Treatment for an IVSR typically involves emergency surgery to repair the tear in the interventricular septum. Incorrect Options: Option A- Aortic dissection : Symptoms of aortic dissection may include sudden onset of severe chest pain, tearing sensation in the chest, radiating pain to the back, abdomen or legs, loss of consciousness, and symptoms of shock. However, the symptoms and clinical findings described in the case do not fit the clinical picture of aortic dissection. Option C - Papillary muscle rupture : Papillary muscle rupture is a rare but potentially life-threatening complication that can occur after myocardial infarction. It can cause mitral regurgitation , leading to hemodynamic instability, symptoms of heart failure, and pulmonary oedema . However, the characteristic murmur in papillary muscle rupture is a holosystolic murmur heard best at the apex , and not a holosystolic murmur heard at the left lower sternal border. Option D - Ventricular wall rupture : Ventricular wall rupture is another rare but serious complication of myocardial infarction, where the infarcted wall of the ventricle ruptures, causing cardiac tamponade . This condition can cause chest pain, shortness of breath, and hemodynamic instability. Due to cardiac tamponade, the heart sounds seem distant and it is a very fatal condition. However, in the case described, the holosystolic murmur at the left lower sternal border on auscultation, accompanied by a thrill, suggests interventricular septum rupture as a more likely diagnosis than ventricular wall rupture. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: A 55-year-old woman suddenly begins to experience chest pain that propagates to her left shoulder. She had a migraine headache and was lying in bed when her symptoms started. She has had similar episodes of chest discomfort, which resolved after a few minutes. For the past 20 years, she has smoked a single pack of cigarettes per day. The only drug she takes is sumatriptan. ST-segment elevations are visible in the frontal leads of an ECG. On two separate blood samples, serum troponins were negative, and 30 minutes later, an ECG revealed no abnormalities. Which of the following treatments is most likely to stop this patient's chest discomfort from happening again?
questions.stemHtml: A 55-year-old woman suddenly begins to experience chest pain that propagates to her left shoulder. She had a migraine headache and was lying in bed when her symptoms started. She has had similar episodes of chest discomfort, which resolved after a few minutes. For the past 20 years, she has smoked a single pack of cigarettes per day. The only drug she takes is sumatriptan. ST-segment elevations are visible in the frontal leads of an ECG. On two separate blood samples, serum troponins were negative, and 30 minutes later, an ECG revealed no abnormalities. Which of the following treatments is most likely to stop this patient's chest discomfort from happening again?
questions.solution: Correct Option A: Diltiazem The first-line therapy for vasospastic angina is calcium channel blockers (CCBs), such as diltiazem. They work well for both prevention and acute assaults . The patient should be counselled to quit smoking, a recognized risk factor for vasospastic angina, and triptans should also be stopped. For the acute abortive therapy of vasospastic angina, nitroglycerin is frequently used. Because of the establishment of nitrate tolerance limits, long-acting nitrates (such as isosorbide mononitrate) are only used as second-line medications for controlling vasospastic episodes. Provocative tests can be used during coronary angiography to detect the existence of vasospastic angina (usually using acetylcholine, less commonly ergonovine or hyperventilation). I ncorrect Options: Option B - Propranolol Propranolol and other nonselective beta-blockers shouldn't be used to treat vasospastic angina because they inhibit the relaxation of vascular smooth muscle cells. Since coronary spasms are primarily caused by smooth muscle cell activation , beta blockers would exacerbate vasospastic angina . However, beta-blockers should be used to manage acute coronary syndrome to lower heart rate and cardiac oxygen consumption. Angina and ST elevations , which are present in this patient, can be symptoms of ACS. However, in STEMI, neither the serum troponin levels nor the ECG would revert to normal after 30 minutes . Option C - Aspirin: Aspirin is used to treat and avoid acute coronary syndrome because it inhibits platelet aggregation. Angina and ST elevations, which are present in this patient, can be symptoms of ACS. However, in STEMI, neither the serum troponin levels nor the ECG would revert to normal after 30 minutes. High-dose aspirin should be avoided in patients with vasospastic angina because it suppresses the production of prostaglandins and may even cause vasospasms. Option D - Clopidogrel: Clopidogrel (P2Y12 receptor antagonists) is not used to treat vasospastic angina because the brief ischemic symptoms observed in this case are caused by vasospasms rather than abnormal platelet aggregation. The acute coronary syndrome is treated with P2Y12 receptor antagonists, typically in conjunction with aspirin, and thrombosis is avoided after stent insertion. Angina and ECG abnormalities like ST elevations, both present in this case, are the manifestations of ACS. However, 30 minutes later, the ECG of a STEMI would still be different. Furthermore, a STEMI would result in elevated troponin T and I, which are absent in this instance. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: A 12-year-old boy is presented to the cardiology centre with complaints of shortness of breath, growth retardation and bluish discolouration of the nails. On examination, clubbing of nails is present. The patient is diagnosed with ventricular septal defect at the age of 12. Which of the following is a clinical feature of ventricular septal defect?
questions.stemHtml: A 12-year-old boy is presented to the cardiology centre with complaints of shortness of breath, growth retardation and bluish discolouration of the nails. On examination, clubbing of nails is present. The patient is diagnosed with ventricular septal defect at the age of 12. Which of the following is a clinical feature of ventricular septal defect?

options.label: D
options.text: Pulse disparity in arms and legs

questions.solution: Correct Option A: Harsh holo-systolic murmur Patients with VSD have a loud harsh holo-systolic blowing murmur that is heard best at the left lower sternal border often a thrill is also associated with it. A defect in the membranous portion of the ventricular septum is the most common form of VSD, the most common congenital heart disease. The anterior side of the septal leaflet of the tricuspid valve in the posteroinferior position is the site of the membranous defect. The apical or mid portion region of the ventricular septum is the site of the muscular-type septal defect. Large VSD is associated with congestive heart failure due to pulmonary hypertension caused by excessive pulmonary blood flow and can present as dyspnea, failure to grow, and pulmonary infections. Chest radiographs and ECG are usually normal in small VSDs but the presence of right ventricular hypertrophy on ECG is a sign of a large defect and shows that the patient probably has pulmonary hypertension. Size and position of the defect are determined by echocardiography and cardiomegaly with prominent atrium and ventricles are common x-ray findings in large defects. Incorrect Options: Option B: Overriding aorta It is a feature of a cyanotic congenital heart disease, the Tetralogy of Fallot, characterized by hypertrophy of the right ventricle, VSD, pulmonary stenosis, and an overriding aorta and occurs due to the anterior deviation of the infundibular septum during cardiac development. The degree of right ventricular outflow tract obstruction determines symptom severity. Signs of heart failure are associated with mild obstruction initially whereas severe obstruction causes cyanosis in infants. Option C: Continuous machine-like murmur It is a feature of the patent ductus arteriosus . Shunting of blood from the aorta to the pulmonary artery occurs due to failure of the ductus arteriosus to close which occurs soon after birth. In full-term infants’ spontaneous closure rarely occurs after a few weeks but it is common in preterm infants. A continuous machinery murmur can be heard in the left second intercostal space that may radiate to the left clavicle or sternal border. Patients can be asymptomatic in small defects, but large defects are associated with heart failure. Option D: Pulse disparity in the arms and legs Coarctation of the aorta is associated with the pulse disparity in the upper and lower extremities. The area of ductus arteriosus below the origin of the left subclavian artery is a common site of the coarctation and symptom relief may be provided in the first few days of life by the patent ductus arteriosus. As the blood supply to the descending aorta depends on collaterals, radio-femoral delay occurs in this condition. In older children, it should be managed by surgical excision and then performing re-anastomosis. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: A 70-year-old man was diagnosed with aortic dissection (type A). He presented with the complaint of severe tearing chest pain and shortness of breath. Which of the following complications can occur in this patient?
questions.stemHtml: A 70-year-old man was diagnosed with aortic dissection (type A). He presented with the complaint of severe tearing chest pain and shortness of breath. Which of the following complications can occur in this patient?
questions.solution: Correct Option B: Aortic regurgitation Type A aortic dissection involves the ascending aorta and can even involve the arch of the aorta and descending aorta. Aortic dissection involving the ascending aorta results in dilatation of the aortic root, which can lead to aortic regurgitation. Patients with aortic regurgitation will present with shortness of breath, irregular pulse, lightheadedness, syncope and palpitations. Incorrect Options: Option A: Aortic stenosis Aortic stenosis does not occur as a complication of type A aortic dissection. Patients with aortic stenosis will present with syncope, angina, shortness of breath and pulsus parvus et tardus( weak pulse with delayed peak). Option C: Coronary steal syndrome Coronary steal syndrome is inconsistent with the complication of aortic dissection. In coronary steal syndrome , there is stenosis of the coronary artery , and the vessels beyond the point of stenosis are maximally dilated. When a vasodilator is given to these patients, it will dilate the normal vessel and divert the blood away from the area supplied by the stenosed vessel . This will further result in ischemia in the area perfused by the stenosed vessels . Option D: Subclavian steal syndrome Subclavian steal syndrome is a potential sign of upper limb peripheral artery disease. When the patient uses his arm , blood is diverted from the brain to the limbs via the vertebral artery, causing the patient to experience cortical blindness, dizziness, and collapse. Subclavian steal syndrome does not occur as a complication of aortic dissection. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stemHtml: A 60-year-old male patient with a history of hypertension and hyperlipidemia presents to the emergency department with worsening pain and swelling in his right groin, which developed after undergoing percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) through the right femoral artery. Physical examination reveals a pulsatile mass in the right groin with surrounding erythema and tenderness. Auscultation of the mass reveals a systolic bruit at the femoral artery puncture site. What is the most likely complication of PCI in this patient?
questions.solution: Correct Option D: Pseudoaneurysm Pseudoaneurysm formation is a rare but potentially serious vascular complication of percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) . It occurs when there is a disruption in the continuity of the vessel wall , resulting in a contained hematoma that communicates with the arterial lumen through a small neck or tract. Pseudoaneurysms can occur at the site of the arterial access or any point along the catheterisation pathway and are most commonly seen after femoral artery access. Symptoms of pseudoaneurysm may include swelling, pain, and a pulsatile mass at the site of the arterial access. Auscultation of the pulsatile mass typically reveals a systolic bruit . In some cases, patients may also experience signs of bleeding, such as hematoma or hypotension. Diagnosis is typically confirmed using Doppler ultrasound , which can identify the characteristic swirling blood flow within the aneurysm sac . If left untreated, pseudoaneurysms can lead to thromboembolism, rupture, or chronic fistula formation. Therefore, timely intervention is important. Management options include conservative observation, ultrasound-guided compression, percutaneous thrombin injection, or surgical repair , depending on the size and location of the aneurysm, the patient's clinical status, and the experience of the treating physician. Incorrect Options: Option A - Hematoma: Hematoma is a common vascular complication after PCI, presenting as localized swelling or bruising without pulsation. Option B - Femoral nerve injury : Femoral nerve injury can occur during vascular access due to the proximity of the nerve to the femoral artery. However, it usually presents with paresthesias and patellar tendon hyporeflexia of the ipsilateral thigh. Option C - Arteriovenous fistula: An arteriovenous fistula is another rare complication that occurs when there is direct communication between the arterial and venous systems, causing the shunting of blood flow. It causes a continuous bruit with a palpable thrill rather than a systolic bruit and does not usually present as a pulsatile mass. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.solution: Correct Option A: Raynaud’s phenomenon Recurrent vasospasm of the fingers and toes , typically in reaction to stress or exposure to cold, is Raynaud's phenomenon. It can happen independently of another illness (Raynaud disease) or in conjunction with it (usually autoimmune). The capillaroscopy results are normal, and the vasospasm is paroxysmal, bilateral, and present. Avoiding triggers , such as cold temperatures, nicotine use, and some medicines, is the main component of management. (e.g., CCBs). Raynaud's phenomenon is caused by exaggerated vasoconstriction of the digital arteries and arterioles in reaction to cold or emotional stress. Raynaud's phenomenon is characterized by a progressive discolouration of fingers and digits from white (ischemia) to blue (hypoxia) to red (reactive hyperemia). This patient most likely has vasospastic angina, linked with other vasospastic disorders such as the Raynaud’s phenomenon. The vascular theory of migraine proposes that dilation and vasoconstriction of intracranial and extracranial arteries contribute to migraine symptoms such as headache and aura. While this theory is no longer widely accepted , vasospasm may still play a part in the development of migraines, and there may be a link between vasospastic angina and migraine. This patient, however, most likely has vasospastic angina , which is not linked with hypertension. This patient, however, is most likely suffering from vasospastic angina unrelated to T2DM. questions.solution: Correct Option C: Sildenafil This patient’s clinical findings and tests indicate idiopathic pulmonary hypertension. Pulmonary hypertension (PH) is a medical condition with abnormally elevated blood pressure in the pulmonary vessels. Idiopathic pulmonary hypertension can be treated with bosentan, sildenafil, and/or epoprostenol. Sildenafil is a phosphodiesterase inhibitor and causes vasodilation . Side effects of sildenafil include headaches, nausea, flushing, dizziness, and indigestion. It is contraindicated in patients who are allergic to this medication. It should be avoided in individuals taking nitrates or having severe liver or cardiac issues. questions.stem: A 38 year old female presents as a new patient to your OPD. She is currently 10 weeks pregnant. She was referred by her gynecologist for evaluation of a murmur. The patient reports mild shortness of breath with moderate exertion but states that this does not limit her exercise ability. A transthoracic echo is performed in the OPD, which demonstrates restricted opening of the mitral valve leaflet tips with a mean trans-mitral gradient of 4 mmHg and a mitral valve area of 1.6 cm2. questions.solution: Correct Option D: Concussion Concussions are classified as mild TBI and present with negative computerized tomography (CT) findings. Headaches, nausea, dizziness, irritability, and impaired ability to concentrate can persist for days after the event. Persistence of these symptoms for weeks is called post concussion syndrome and can last from one month to a year. Using PECARN algorithm and shared decision making, it is reasonable not to CT scan this child’s head. Incorrect Options: Option A - Contusion: A contusion is an injury to the brain tissue that results in leakage of small blood vessels. Option B - Epidural hematoma: An epidural hematoma is typically the result large traumatic force to the temporal surface of the skull damaging the middle meningeal artery. These patients present can with transient LOC followed by sudden collapse. This is unlikely in this patient. Option C - Subarachnoid hemorrhage: A subarachnoid hemorrhage is usually the result of an aneurysmal bleed in the circle of Willis. Blood collects in the subarachnoid space. @Neet_pg_bot

Soon after, ECG shows prominent U wave in leads II, III and AVF. Which of the following will most likely treat patient’s ECG findings?

Patient’s potassium is 3.4 meq/L, blood sugar is 475 mg/dl, anion gap is 28 and ABG shows a pH of 7.21. Urine is positive for ketones. Patient is given 10 units of regular insulin immediately. Soon after, ECG shows prominent U wave in leads II, III and AVF. Which of the following will most likely treat patient’s ECG findings?
questions.solution: Correct Option C: IV potassium Patient’s U waves are most likely from hypokalemia , as this occurred after administration of insulin. Though serum potassium may be normal or even elevated initially in DKA, patients have a total potassium deficit. Therefore, when patient was given subcutaneous insulin, patient’s hypokalemia worsened. This causes prolonged ventricular repolarization and prominent U waves. If untreated patient is at increased risk of torsades de pointes. Incorrect Options: Option A - Insulin drip: This patient has diabetic ketoacidosis (DKA) and will require an insulin drip. However, that will not treat patient’s U waves, which is most likely from hypokalemia in this patient. Starting an insulin drip without repleting potassium will worsen hypokalemia as insulin drives potassium intracellularly. Option B - IV fluids: This patient is hypotensive but should receive IV fluid boluses as he is volume-depleted from decreased oral intake and hyperglycemia. However, this will not treat’s patient’s U wave. Option D - IV phosphorus: Patients in DKA are at risk for hypophosphatemia, however, this does not cause U waves to occur. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.answerText: The American College of Cardiology / American Heart Association recommends viability testing when planning revascularization
questions.solution: Correct Option A: The American College of Cariology / American Heart Association recommends viability testing when planning revascularization The most recent (2013) guidelines by the American College of Cardiology / American Heart Association give a class IIa (level of evidence B) recommendation for viability testing in heart failure, stating that such testing “is reasonable in select situation when planning revascularization of any kind”. Of note, this recommendation was given after the STICH trial in which patients who had viability assessed by dobutamine echocardiography or SPECT imaging showed to difference in outcome based on the interaction between treatment allocation and the presence of absence of viability. Therefore, most experts agree that for the patient at relatively high surgical risk the demonstration of significant residual myocardial viability may tilt the risk benefit ratio more in favor for surgery. Incorrect Options: Option B- Use of thallium – 201 is associated with improved sensitivity for the detection of myocardial viability when compared to Tc-99m sestamibi: Clinical studies have not shown superiority of one perfusion tracer (i.e. thallium -201, Tc-99m sestambi, or Tc-99m tetrofosmin) over the others for viability assessment Option C- The uptake of thallium – 201 across myocytes cell membranes is by passive diffusion: Technetium – 99m (Tc-99m) sestambi and Tc-99m tetofosmin are Tc-99m labelled radiotracers whose uptake across myocyte cell membranes is by passive diffusion. This is in contrast to the uptake of thallium – 201 which is active. Option D- A potential advantage of thallium – 201 over Tc-99m is the ability to get better quality gated images: Because of this, additive information on regional function can be gained, and applied to line source attenuation correction with gadolinium 153 in order to improve adjundication of inferior attenuation artifacts. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.solution: Correct Option C: IV rasburicase Tumor lysis syndrome (TLS) is an oncologic emergency occurring primarily in patients with acute leukemia, lymphomas, and rapidly proliferating tumors. However, it has been reported in other cancers rarely associated with TLS such as endometrial cancer, hepatocellular carcinoma, chronic lymphocytic leukemia, and chronic myelogenous leukemia. In principle, as effective anticancer therapy is delivered, tumors with greater mass carry a greater potential to release more cell contents, increasing the risk of TLS. Two or more of the characteristic electrolyte or metabolic disturbances within 24 hours are diagnostic for TLS. These include hyperuricemia (>8.0 mg/dL), hyperkalemia (>6.0 mmol/L), hyperphosphatemia (>4.5 mg/dL), hypocalcemia (<7.0 mg/dL), and renal impairment (defined as serum creatinine 0.3 mg/dL above baseline for age-appropriate normal range). Patients present with symptoms consistent with these derangements (e.g. nausea, vomiting, lethargy, malaise, oliguria, hematuria, peripheral edema). Complications that may arise include cardiac arrhythmias, worsening renal failure, seizure, and ultimately death without prompt treatment. Treatment includes the correction of electrolyte abnormalities and IV hydration to increase renal perfusion and minimize acidosis. Acidosis promotes uric acid crystal precipitation. Loop diuretics such as furosemide are sometimes used in this setting. IV rasburicase at 0.2 mg/kg should be administered if the patient was not pretreated. Rasburicase has been shown in randomized clinical trials to have a greater effect than allopurinol in lowering serum phosphorus and improving serum creatinine and uric acid levels. Incorrect Options: Option A - Antibiotics to treat urinary pathogens: Antibiotics are not indicated for treatment of tumor lysis syndrome. Option B - Thiazide diuretics: A thiazide diuretic would exacerbate TLS, as thiazides compete with uric acid for renal tubule secretion and reduce renal clearance of uric acid. Option D - Renal replacement therapy: Renal replacement therapy should be considered if the patient does not respond to initial treatments, has symptomatic hypocalcemia induced by hyperphosphatemia, anuria, oliguria, or a calcium-phosphate product of 70 mg 2 dL 2 . @Neet_pg_bot

questions.solution: Correct Option C: Scabies Scabies is caused by the itch mite, Sarcoptes scabiei, an ectoparasite acquired by humans from close physical contact. The gravid female mite will burrow under the skin and deposit eggs and excrement. Three to ten days after exposure, the human host will develop a hypersensitivity reaction to the mite, ova, and excrement, at which time intense pruritus, characteristically worse at night, will begin. Burrows (linear tracks of the progression of the mite) are characteristic of scabies; papules, vesicles, and pustules are also seen. Constitutional symptoms are rare in the absence of bacterial superinfection. Lesions can occur on the scalp, face, extremities (including the palms and soles and characteristically featuring burrows at the web spaces of the fingers), chest, back, abdomen, and genitalia, although the lesions are usually not present above the neck in patients older than 5 years. Incorrect Options: Option A - Pediculosis corporis: Pediculosis corporis (infestation with body lice) does not produce a rash (save for that caused by excoriation). Option B -Tinea corporis: Tinea corporis (ringworm) features reddish, circular lesions with a surrounding collar of vesicles. Option D -Varicella: Varicella does feature a progression from papules to vesicles to pustules, but not burrows, and is a febrile illness. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: A 5-year-old boy presents with right knee pain and a limp. He has no history of trauma. His hip is abducted and externally rotated,with exacerbation of pain with internal rotation. What is the most likely cause of this symptom?
questions.stemHtml: A 5-year-old boy presents with right knee pain and a limp. He has no history of trauma. His hip is abducted and externally rotated,with exacerbation of pain with internal rotation. What is the most likely cause of this symptom?
questions.solution: Correct Option C: Transient synovitis Transient synovitis and septic arthritis are the most common causes of atraumatic hip pain in children. Transient synovitis usually occurs in children between the ages of 3 and 8 years of age, most often in boys. Children typically have had symptoms for one to three days at presentation and will demonstrate an antalgic gait with an abducted and externally rotated hip at rest. Pain is exacerbated with internal rotation of the hip, although pain with motion is less severe than in children with septic arthritis of the hip. Referred pain to the knee may be the only complaint, so careful inspection of the hip is mandatory in all patients with isolated knee pain. Referred pain from the hip to knee is usually a dull pain that is located anteriorly and does not localize to bone or soft tissue. Examination of the knee is usually normal. The hip exam typically demonstrates a limited range of motion with pain. Serious causes of hip pain must be excluded, including septic arthritis, fracture, slipped capital femoral epiphysis (SCFE), and Legg-Calve-Perthes disease). Patients with transient synovitis rarely have a fever Management of transient synovitis is purely supportive and includes rest and NSAIDs. Incorrect Options: Option A - Femoral neck fracture: Hip fracture in a paediatric patient is suggested by high-force trauma, and severe tenderness is common. Option B - Osteogenesis imperfecta: Osteogenesis imperfecta is a rare disease that causes problems in bone synthesis due to collagen defects. Frequent fractures are common, and a physical examination may demonstrate blue sclerae, deafness, and ligamentous laxity. Subclinical cases may be more common than previously recognized. Option D - Slipped capital femoral epiphysis (SCFE): SCFE occurs when the femoral epiphysis slips off the metaphysis, usually in adolescents. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.solution: Correct Option C: 1 mg of glucagon intravenously Concurrent use of beta-blockers (metroprolol, in this case) is a risk factor for more severe anaphylactic reactions. Patients who are on a beta-blocker and have reactions that are refractory to the administration of epinephrine and fluid resuscitation should receive a 1-5 mg bolus of glucagon. This can be followed with an infusion of 5-15 mcg of glucagon per minute. Incorrect Options: Option A - 4 units of fresh frozen plasma: Fresh frozen plasma is used to treat hereditary angioedema but would be of no use in a case of anaphylaxis. Option B - 50 mg of diphenhydramine intravenously: Antihistamines are effective for pruritis and hives related to allergic reactions. While they are commonly administered in anaphylaxis, they are not effective treatment for hypotension or airway obstruction. Option D - 125mg of methylprednisolone intravenously: Glucocorticoids have a delayed onset of action and have not been shown to be of benefit for the acute signs and symptoms of anaphylaxis, though they are commonly given. @Neet_pg_bot

Neurologic exam reveals a normal cranial nerve exam with normal and symmetric reflexes. Visual fields are intact. The patient denies abdominal pain and has no palpable organomegaly. Blood work reveals a normal platelet count and a normal hepatic function panel. The patient begins to have generalized tonic-clonic activity. After administering benzodiazepines, what should be performed to make the diagnosis?

questions.solution: Correct Option B: MR venogram This patient has a cerebral venous thrombosis (CVT). CVTs are more common in women than men and may be infectious (e.g., associated with meningitis, otitis media, facial cellulitis) or non-infectious. Non-infectious causes include direct insult from trauma or surgery, dehydration, or a hypercoagulable state (e.g., peripartum, oral contraceptive pill use). Headache is the primary presenting feature. Papilledema may be present, and seizures occur in up to 50% of patients. Diagnosis is often delayed, so a high clinical index of suspicion is needed. Diagnostic accuracy is best with magnetic resonance (MR) venography. Initial management is with heparin. Incorrect Options: Option A - CT head without contrast: Although a CT of the patient's head without contrast may show findings suggestive of CVT (e.g., hyperdensity of a thrombosed vessel, cerebral edema), it is neither sensitive nor specific enough to confirm or exclude the diagnosis. Option C - Lumbar puncture: A lumbar puncture may be performed to evaluate potential causes of seizure, including subarachnoid hemorrhage or infectious causes (e.g., herpes encephalitis, meningitis). However, this patient’s symptoms were gradual in onset, and she has no neurologic deficits or meningeal signs. Furthermore, she is afebrile with otherwise normal vital signs. Her presentation makes subarachnoid hemorrhage or meningitis less likely, reducing the utility of a lumbar puncture. Option D - Magnesium sulfate bolus: Intravenous magnesium sulfate is the treatment for eclampsia, a peripartum seizure disorder that includes the features of preeclampsia (hypertension and proteinuria). HELLP syndrome (hemolytic anemia, elevated liver enzymes, and low platelets) is a specific pregnancy-related syndrome that may precede eclampsia. However, this patient has a normal blood pressure and normal blood test results, making eclampsia or HELLP syndrome less likely. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.solution: Correct Option B: Staphylococcus aureus This patient has food poisoning caused by Staphylococcus aureus . The rapid onset of symptoms after exposure suggests the ingestion of a toxin rather than infection by a toxin-producing bacterium. Staphylococcus aureus or Bacillus cereus can cause these symptoms, which resemble viral gastroenteritis. Typically, vomiting is more prominent than diarrhea. Bacteria that colonize and produce toxins (e.g., enterotoxigenic E. coli ) or that damage cell walls (e.g., Salmonella) require one to several days from exposure to symptoms. Option D - Giardia lamblia: Giardia lamblia typically produces large amounts of watery diarrhea. It is common in the United States, especially in daycare settings. Symptoms typically occur 1 to 2 weeks after exposure with bloating, abdominal pain, and foul-smelling stools. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.solution: Correct Option B: Cyclophosphamide Non-Hodgkin's lymphoma is typically treated with a regimen called R-CHOP: rituximab, cyclophosphamide, doxorubicin (also known as hydroxydaunomycin), vincristine (also known as Oncovin), and prednisone. Cyclophosphamide causes hemorrhagic cystitis, as experienced by this patient. Cyclophosphamide can also cause hair loss, vomiting, myelosuppression, and nephrotoxicity. Incorrect Options: Option A - Vincristine: Vincristine causes peripheral neuropathy, not hemorrhagic cystitis. Other side effects include mucositis, myelosuppression, vomiting, and the development of radiation dermatitis. Option D - Methotrexate: Methotrexate can damage the lungs, causing interstitial pneumonitis, alveolitis, or pulmonary fibrosis. If given in high doses with cisplatin, methotrexate can damage the renal tubules. Other side effects of methotrexate include mucositis, vomiting, photosensitivity, hepatitis, myelosuppression, and stroke-like syndrome. @Neet_pg_bot

He is emergently intubated. He has been on the ventilator and suddenly decompensates. HR is 160 and BP of 79/44 with maintained SpO2 at 95%. Which of the following is the most appropriate?
questions.stemHtml: A 72-year-old male with COPD presents with shortness of breath, fevers, and coughing. The patient is extremely short of breath and hypoxic with very little air movement. He is emergently intubated. He has been on the ventilator and suddenly decompensates. HR is 160 and BP of 79/44 with maintained SpO2 at 95%. Which of the following is the most appropriate?

options.label: A
options.text: Disconnect the patient from the ventilator and use Ambu bag to provide positive pressure ventilation

options.label: C
options.text: Place orogastric tube for gastric decompression

questions.answerText: Disconnect the patient from the ventilator and use Ambu bag to provide positive pressure ventilation
questions.solution: Correct Option A: Disconnect the patient from the ventilator and use Ambu bag to provide positive pressure ventilation A complication of invasive ventilation is the development of auto-PEEP or intrinsic PEEP. This is a more common problem of those with obstructive lung disease due to prolonged expiratory phase. Intrinsic PEEP accumulates when the patient is unable to fully exhale and there is residual volume left that continues to amass. When there is significant auto-PEEP, then acute hypotension may be precipitated due to increased intrathoracic pressures. This should resolve rather quickly once the patient is disconnected from the ventilator. If there is no improvement then auto-PEEP is likely not the culprit and tension pneumothorax should quickly be evaluated for. Mnemonic to troubleshoot ventilators: D isplacement of tube or cuff O bstruction of tube/circuit P neumothorax E quipment failure S tacked breaths Incorrect Options: Option B - Tube thoracostomy for tension pneumothorax: Tube thoracostomy would be secondary to needle decompression if there is emergent concern of tension pneumothorax. Option C - Place orogastric tube for gastric decompression: Gastric decompression is not the cause of abrupt decompensation as seen here, especially given the hypotension. Option D - Start vasopressors: Vasopressors do not address the issue causing hypotension. @Neet_pg_bot

Intrinsic PEEP accumulates when the patient is unable to fully exhale and there is residual volume left that continues to amass. When there is significant auto-PEEP, then acute hypotension may be precipitated due to increased intrathoracic pressures. This should resolve rather quickly once the patient is disconnected from the ventilator. If there is no improvement then auto-PEEP is likely not the culprit and tension pneumothorax should quickly be evaluated for.
  • Mnemonic to troubleshoot ventilators:
    • Displacement of tube or cuff
    • Obstruction of tube/circuit
    • Pneumothorax
    • Equipment failure
    • Stacked breaths

Incorrect Options:

Option B - Tube thoracostomy for tension pneumothorax: Tube thoracostomy would be secondary to needle decompression if there is emergent concern of tension pneumothorax.

His blood pressure is 100/80 mmHg, respiratory rate is 11 breaths/minute, and heart rate is 60 beats/minute. Pupils are constricted and bowel sounds are decreased. Which of the following is the most appropriate initial medication to administer?
questions.stemHtml: A 40-year-old man with a history of substance use disorder is transported to the emergency department by his wife. Upon arrival, he is somnolent and difficult to arouse. His blood pressure is 100/80 mmHg, respiratory rate is 11 breaths/minute, and heart rate is 60 beats/minute. Pupils are constricted and bowel sounds are decreased. Which of the following is the most appropriate initial medication to administer?
questions.solution: Correct Option D: Naloxone This patient is suffering from opioid intoxication, as indicated by his clinical presentation. Signs of opioid intoxication include depressed mental status, miosis, decreased respiratory rate and tidal volume; decreased bowel sounds, nausea, vomiting, and severe itching. The patient's heart rate can be normal to low. Hypotension may occur as a result of histamine release, but it is not consistently seen. Overdose that involves opioid drugs is a life-threatening situation. Fatal respiratory depression can occur due to direct suppression of respiratory centres in the midbrain and medulla. Naloxone is a strong antagonist of µ-opioid receptors, a medium antagonist of kappa-opioid receptors, and a weak antagonist of delta-opioid receptors. Opioid intoxication is treated with naloxone, adequate hydration, mechanical ventilation. Incorrect Options: Option A - Acamprosate: Acamprosate is an anti-craving drug used for maintenance therapy of alcohol withdrawal. Option B - Bupropion: Bupropion is used for nicotine withdrawal and acts on dopamine and noradrenaline receptors. Option C - Buprenorphine: Buprenorphine is used for detoxification and as part of maintenance therapy for opioid withdrawal. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: A family brings their two-year-old child into the pediatrician’s OPD for a “white glow” that they noticed in their child’s left eye over the past two months. The child is otherwise healthy. Family history is unremarkable. There is no history of trauma. On exam, there is an orange red reflection in the child’s right pupil. There is a white reflection from the left pupil. The first mutation leading to this patient’s condition most likely occurred in which of the following?
questions.stemHtml:
A family brings their two-year-old child into the pediatrician’s OPD for a “white glow” that they noticed in their child’s left eye over the past two months. The child is otherwise healthy. Family history is unremarkable. There is no history of trauma. On exam, there is an orange red reflection in the child’s right pupil. There is a white reflection from the left pupil.
The first mutation leading to this patient’s condition most likely occurred in which of the following?
questions.solution: Correct Option B: The child’s somatic cell Retinoblastoma is high on the differential for a child presenting with leukocoria (abnormal white reflex). In most cases unilateral retinoblastoma is not genetically inherited. Two active copies of the retinoblastoma gene ( RB1 ) are present in cells. The first mutation occurs in either a somatic or a germline cell. The second mutation only occurs in somatic cells (known as the “two hit” hypothesis). Both must be mutated for the clinical manifestations of retinoblastoma to develop. Bilateral retinoblastoma (bilateral leukocoria) frequently suggests a germline mutation, or a mutation in all cells. Patients with this hereditary germline form are also at risk for other cancers, such as pineoblastoma, soft tissue sarcomas, and melanoma. Incorrect Options: Option A - RB enzyme: RB is a tumor suppressor gene. It encodes for a protein that inhibits progression of the cell cycle until a cell is ready to divide. Option C -Mitochondrial DNA: Retinoblastoma is not a mitochondrial disease. Examples of mitochondrial diseases are Kearns-Sayre syndrome, myoclonus epilepsy with ragged-red fibers, and mitochondrial encephalomyopathy with lactic acidosis and stroke-like episodes (MELAS syndrome). Option D - Diploid zygote: The vignette most likely refers to a somatic mutation (not germline) and therefore this mutation would not be expected to be found in the diploid zygote (fusion of two gametes). @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stemHtml: A 50-year-old female undergoes a transabdominal ultrasound for evaluation of periodic episodes of vague right upper quadrant pain. She is noted to have a 21 mm hyperechoic mass protruding into the lumen of the gallbladder. Which of the following is indicated for the management of this patient?
questions.solution: Correct Option A: Open cholecystectomy Malignant gallbladder polyps are more prevalent in patients over the age of 50. Other factors associated with malignancy include size greater than 1.5 cm and solitary sessile hypoechogenic polyps. Polyps that are smaller than 1 cm and asymptomatic can be monitored by ultrasound in 6 to 12 months. Fast-growing polyps; polyps that are wide-based, sessile, or have long pedicles; and those in patients over 50 or with concurrent gallstones are indications for cholecystectomy. In patients with polyps greater than 18 mm in size, open cholecystectomy with possible partial liver resection and possible lymph node dissection is recommended. Incorrect Options: Option B - Laparoscopic cholecystectomy: Laparoscopic cholecystectomy is inadequate for polyps greater than 18 mm in size due to the high risk of malignancy. Option C - Follow-up surveillance in 6 months: Follow-up surveillance within 12 months is only appropriate for small polyps that are asymptomatic. Option D - No follow-up: The goal of management of gallbladder polyps is preventing the development of gallbladder carcinoma @Neet_pg_bot

questions.solution: Correct Option D: Eosinophilic esophagitis TRUE: The differential diagnosis for dysphagia in children should include eosinophilic esophagitis, reflux esophagitis, esophageal motility disorders, and esophageal strictures. GERD is characterized by mucosal injury and esophageal breaks. questions.stem: A mutation in the JAG1 gene is associated with which of the following congenital conditions affecting the biliary tract?
questions.stemHtml: A mutation in the JAG1 gene is associated with which of the following congenital conditions affecting the biliary tract?
questions.solution: Correct Option C: Alagille syndrome TRUE: Alagille syndrome is characterized by a paucity of interlobular bile ducts. Cholestasis, pulmonic stenosis, dysmorphic facies, butterfly vertebrae, and renal dysplasia are also associated with Alagille syndrome. Patients often have short stature and may have developmental delay. Mutations in the JAG1 gene are associated with more than 90% of cases and are transmitted through autosomal dominant inheritance. Cholestatic liver disease severity is variable, and management may range from conservative treatment for symptoms like pruritus to liver transplantation in 20% of patients who develop end-stage renal disease. Incorrect Options: Option A- Caroli disease: FALSE: Caroli disease is associated with the PKHD1 gene, which is primarily expressed in the kidneys in addition to the liver, pancreas, and lungs. It is characterized by dilation of intrahepatic bile ducts. Option B-Progressive familial intrahepatic cholestasis type 2: FALSE : Progressive familial intrahepatic cholestasis type 2 is the most common type of PFIC and is caused by mutations in ABCB11. Option D-Mirizzi syndrome: FALSE: Mirizzi syndrome refers to a complication of cholelithiasis in which impaction of a gallstone in the cystic duct causes compression of the common hepatic duct or common bile duct. @Neet_pg_bot

Transabdominal ultrasound of the right upper quadrant reveals gallbladder sludge, with a 5 mm hyperechoic mass projecting into the gallbladder lumen. Which of the following is appropriate for management?
questions.stemHtml: A 38-year-old female is evaluated for periodic episodes of nausea and mild to moderate nonspecific right sided abdominal pain. Transabdominal ultrasound of the right upper quadrant reveals gallbladder sludge, with a 5 mm hyperechoic mass projecting into the gallbladder lumen. Which of the following is appropriate for management?
questions.solution: Correct Option A: Follow-up ultrasound in 6 months Gallbladder polyps are commonly found on routine abdominal ultrasound. In most cases, they are benign polyps, but some will progress to gallbladder cancer. Management of gallbladder polyps is based on available evidence of clinical characteristics that suggest increased risk for malignancy. Patient risk factors for malignant polyps include age over 60, presence of gallstones, and primary sclerosing cholangitis. Polyp characteristics associated with higher risk are sessile morphology, size over 6 mm, and solitary polyps. Patients with polyps who have symptoms that are suggestive of biliary colic should generally undergo cholecystectomy. This patient has non-specific symptoms and a polyp that is 5 mm. Although there is no consensus on the time to follow-up, some experts recommend an initial follow-up at 3 months for polyps 6-9 mm in asymptomatic patients without signs of malignancy. At that time, if no significant change is noted, follow- up in 12 months is recommended. This patient has non-specific symptoms and can undergo follow-up in 6 months. Incorrect Options: Option B - Laparoscopic cholecystectomy: Fast-growing polyps, polyps that are wide-based, sessile, or have long pedicles, and those in patients over 50 or with concurrent gallstones are indications for cholecystectomy. Polyps between 10-20 mm in diameter should be regarded as possibly malignant, and a cholecystectomy with full thickness dissection is recommended. Option C - Obtain CEA and CA 19-9: Tumor marker levels are not useful for differentiating malignant and benign polyps. Open D - Open cholecystectomy: In patients with polyps greater than 18 mm in size, open cholecystectomy with is indicated. @Neet_pg_bot

questions.stem: A 22-year-old female at 32 weeks of gestation presents with malaise, nausea, vomiting, and abdominal pain for 3 days. She has otherwise been healthy, and her pregnancy has been without complications. Vital signs are Temperature 98.6°F, BP 138/92 mmHg, heart rate 93/minute, and RR 16/minute. On exam, she is jaundiced and appears acutely ill. Although she is oriented, she is noticeably slow answering questions. Her abdomen is gravid, and exam also reveals mild pitting edema in both ankles. Laboratory studies reveal total bilirubin 11 mg/dL, direct bilirubin 8 mg/dL, ALP 330 U/L. AST 440 U/L, ALT 530 U/L, glucose 80 mg/dL, and creatinine 1.4 mg/dL. Albumin is 2.7 g/L, and WBC count is 20,000/mm^3 with platelets 88,000/mm^3 and INR 2.8. Which of the following is appropriate for the evaluation and management of this patient?

Laboratory studies reveal total bilirubin 11 mg/dL, direct bilirubin 8 mg/dL, ALP 330 U/L. AST 440 U/L, ALT 530 U/L, glucose 80 mg/dL, and creatinine 1.4 mg/dL. questions.solution: D. Maternal stabilization and urgent delivery This presentation suggests AFLP. It is a rare disorder, occurring in 1 in 20,000 deliveries. It is associated with low maternal weight. Acute fatty liver of pregnancy usually occurs in the third trimester, and common symptoms include nausea or vomiting with abdominal pain, anorexia, and jaundice. Patients may have signs of preeclampsia. Extrahepatic complications include central diabetes insipidus and pancreatitis. Serum aminotransferase levels are elevated, usually no more than 500 U/L, and serum bilirubin is also elevated. Platelets may be decreased, and WBC may be elevated. Patients with severe disease may have increased prothrombin time, hypoglycemia, acute kidney injury, hyperuricemia, or elevated serum ammonia. The treatment is maternal stabilization and prompt delivery. Incorrect Options: Option A - CT of the Abdomen: The presentation is consistent with AFLP, and maternal stabilization with urgent delivery is indicated, although CT should be done to rule out subcapsular hematoma before delivery in a stable patient. Option B -UDCA: UDCA has no role in the treatment of acute fatty liver of pregnancy. Option C - Liver Ultrasound: Imaging studies of the liver to exclude other diagnoses may be necessary when the diagnosis is unclear, but in this case the best option is maternal stabilization and delivery. @Neet_pg_bot

Past medical history is significant for CAD since 4 years. She underwent CABG at that admission. Examination reveals dry mucous membranes and tenting of the skin. BUN is 28 mg/dL, and creatinine is 1.4 mg/dL. HCO3 is 12. Serum lactate is 8 mmol/L, and pH is 7.30. Arteriogram reveals superior mesenteric artery ischemia, and the patient is taken to surgery for exploratory laparotomy with planned resection of ischemic segments of small bowel. Which of the following is true concerning her postoperative digestive capacity?
